BESTOWAL OF TITLE "RIGHT HONOURABLE"
speechtext:
1.	Has the Prime Minister requested Her Majesty the Queen to give approval to the designation or title of "Right Honourable" being made available to any Canadian or Canadians although such person or persons are not members of Her Majesty's imperial privy council?
2.	Has any order in council to such effect been passed?
3.	If not, what is the authority on which such action is based?
4.	Is it the intention of the government of Canada to deny Canadians hereafter appointment to Her Majesty's imperial privy council?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: BESTOWAL OF TITLE "RIGHT HONOURABLE"
speechtext:
The answer to the first part of the question is that before the appointment of the present Governor General I petitioned the Queen to approve a change in the table of titles for Canada to provide that henceforth the Governor General of Canada shall carry the title "Right Honourable" for life.
Questions
The answer to the second part of the question is no.
The answer to the third part is, the change falls within the area of the royal prerogative in which the sovereign acts on the advice of the prime minister.
The answer to the fourth part of the question is, membership in "Her Majesty's Most Honourable Privy Council" is on the recommendation of the prime minister of Britain since it is technically the privy council of Britain. There has been no decision to deny Canadians appointment to the British privy council if at any time a prime minister of Britain were to wish to recommend such an appointment, just as there has been no decision to alter the practice by which United Kingdom citizens have, on occasion, been offered membership in the Canadian privy council.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. J. Benson (Minister of National Revenue and President of the Treasury Board):
speakerposition: President of the Treasury Board; Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: POLICY RESPECTING PURCHASE OF CANADIAN PRODUCTS
speechtext: The purchasing policy of the Canadian government is consistent with that of foreign governments concerning preferential treatment accorded to domestic industries. Canadian experience indicates that foreign governments direct procurement to their own industry or give their industry preference over Canadian suppliers, in some cases. Canada follows the same practice by giving preference to Canadian industry when there is a need to maintain a Canadian source for strategic reasons or when there is a unique capability in Canada, and always provided it is not necessary to pay excessive premiums in order to buy in Canada.

speechtext:
I should like to ask the

June 12, 1967
Inquiries of the Ministry Prime Minister what Canada's position is regarding the stand announced by Israel through Premier Levi Eshkol to the effect that Israel will not agree to revert to the situation which existed with respect to boundaries until a week ago? Will the Prime Minister tell the people whether Canada intends to stand with Israel in this regard?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-POSITION OF ISRAEL RESPECTING BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it would of course be quite premature to attempt to answer a question of that kind, which would depend on so many circumstances. However, I can say that I think Israel is quite entitled to receive from the international community a greater guarantee of her security than she has had in the past.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-POSITION OF ISRAEL RESPECTING BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the Prime Minister say what instructions are being given to the Canadian ambassador to the United Nations on the Russian resolution which provides that the Israelis shall withdraw to the former boundaries, or those in existence when hostilities broke out?

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-POSITION OF ISRAEL RESPECTING BOUNDARIES
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker, I cannot deal with that subject until it appears before the security council. It has not been considered yet by the security council, so I cannot go beyond the answer I gave my right hon. friend in regard to the commitments which the Israelis are undoubtedly entitled to receive from the international community and the security council, which would give her greater security than she has had in the past.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-POSITION OF ISRAEL RESPECTING BOUNDARIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct my question to the Prime Minister. Has any attempt been made to implement the suggestion, apparently made first by India and then by Canada, that the secretary general of the United Nations send a special representative to attempt conciliation talks between Israel and the Arabs?

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-POSITION OF ISRAEL RESPECTING BOUNDARIES
speechtext: I think, Mr. Speaker, that one of the resolutions before the security council has now dealt with the matter in a limited and brief but not direct way. I know it is being considered at the United Nations whether it would be desirable for the secretary general or someone designated by him or responsible to him to go to the Middle East at the earliest possible date to see whether it would be possible to accomplish the purposes which my hon. friend mentioned.

subtopic: VIET NAM-REPRESENTATIONS FROM VOICE OF WOMEN

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: VIET NAM-REPRESENTATIONS FROM VOICE OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Prime Minister whether today he received representations from the Voice of Women organization with reference to the world situation, particularly with reference to the war in Viet Nam.
Can the Prime Minister also tell the house whether the Canadian government intends to make any further representations to the government of the United States and the government of Hanoi in the hope of bringing about a settlement there? In addition, in view of the fact that the security council has had some success in bringing about at least a cessation of hostilities in the Middle East, would the Canadian government consider trying to have the security council interest itself in bringing about a similar settlement in Viet Nam?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: VIET NAM-REPRESENTATIONS FROM VOICE OF WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that a delegation from the Voice of Women organization was received this morning by the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the absence of the minister, who is attending a meeting of the NATO council. I understand that the representations they made at that time are being referred to me this afternoon, and of course I will consider them.
So far as the last part of the question is concerned, which asked whether the security council could not take cognizance of this situation, my hon. friend knows that several efforts have been made in the past to bring the Viet Nam question before the United Nations or the security council. There are some very real difficulties in the way of doing this, the North Vietnamese having shown no inclination to go to the security council or the United Nations because, of course, they are not a member of that organization.

subtopic: VIET NAM-REPRESENTATIONS FROM VOICE OF WOMEN
speechtext:
A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In view of the fact that Canada is a member of the international control commission, would the Prime Minister take under serious consideration the advisability of Canada raising this matter in the security council, of which Canada is a member, in the hope that this might bring the two parties together for some discussions within the security council?
June 12, 19S7

subtopic: VIET NAM-REPRESENTATIONS FROM VOICE OF WOMEN
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to think this matter could be brought before the security council or some other agency of the United Nations, even the general assembly; but I know that whenever efforts were made in past months to accomplish this they were not successful. I would be very glad to look into the possibility again.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: MR. MCINTOSH-ATTRIBUTION TO PRIME MINISTER OF REMARK IN DEBATE
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege. It was brought to my mind by the refusal of the Chair to allow a question directed to the Prime Minister by my hon. friend from Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare. If everything is to be done according to the rules and regulations I will raise my question of privilege, and it is this. As reported at page 1340 of Hansard, June 9, 1967 a question was asked in this house by the Leader of the Opposition as follows:
I do not know whether the Prime Minister heard the question I asked a while ago. I now ask him specifically, in view of the fact that the statutes of Canada refer to July 1 as Dominion day and he this morning called it Confederation day, does this mean more chiselling away of part of our heritage, when the government refers to this as Confederation day without a decision of parliament?
The Prime Minister answered:
Mr. Speaker, I really cannot answer such a picayune, chiselling question.
The report continues:

subtopic: MR. MCINTOSH-ATTRIBUTION TO PRIME MINISTER OF REMARK IN DEBATE
speechtext: I ask the Prime Minister this question, which is not to be answered by facetious attempts at wit. Is the "Dominion" in Dominion day a dirty word now?

subtopic: MR. MCINTOSH-ATTRIBUTION TO PRIME MINISTER OF REMARK IN DEBATE
speechtext: It could be.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MR. MCINTOSH-ATTRIBUTION TO PRIME MINISTER OF REMARK IN DEBATE
speechtext: I did not say that.

subtopic: MR. MCINTOSH-ATTRIBUTION TO PRIME MINISTER OF REMARK IN DEBATE
speechtext: I heard it and saw it.

subtopic: MR. MCINTOSH-ATTRIBUTION TO PRIME MINISTER OF REMARK IN DEBATE
speechtext: On a question of privilege, I made no such observation and the hon. member has no right to say I did. He had better withdraw this allegation.

subtopic: MR. MCINTOSH-ATTRIBUTION TO PRIME MINISTER OF REMARK IN DEBATE
speechtext: I am surprised the Prime Minister should get up in this house and refuse to back up the words he used when he was sitting in his seat.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. MCINTOSH-ATTRIBUTION TO PRIME MINISTER OF REMARK IN DEBATE
speechtext:
Order. When an hon. member states he heard another hon. member utter certain words and the other hon. member says he did not utter them, there is not very much that can be done about the situation. The rule of the house is that we have to accept the word of an hon. member. We have to accept the word of the hon. member that he heard certain words uttered, and the statement of the other hon. member that he did not utter those words. I would say that the Chair can certainly do nothing.

June 12. 1967

subtopic: EGYPT-CLOSING OF PART OF CANADIAN EMBASSY IN CAIRO

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: EGYPT-CLOSING OF PART OF CANADIAN EMBASSY IN CAIRO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to ask the Prime Minister whether today's report is true that the Egyptian government has forced the closing of part of the Canadian embassy in Cairo. If it is true, has the government of Egypt given the government of Canada any explanation, and what steps is the government taking?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: EGYPT-CLOSING OF PART OF CANADIAN EMBASSY IN CAIRO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the United Arab Republic authorities asked our embassy a few days ago to remove part of the embassy staff from our chancery as a precautionary measure in view of widespread demonstrations. The embassy continued to function with reduced staff, and according to the latest information from our ambassador the embassy
June 12, 1967

is now functioning normally and all members are safe and well.

subtopic: EGYPT-CLOSING OF PART OF CANADIAN EMBASSY IN CAIRO
speechtext: As a supplementary question, has the Prime Minister any word that this action was taken because the Canadian embassy was carrying on some of the normal functions of the embassy of Great Britain due to the lack of diplomatic relations between those two countries?

subtopic: EGYPT-CLOSING OF PART OF CANADIAN EMBASSY IN CAIRO
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, for some months now, as my hon. friend knows, we have been looking after British interests in Cairo, and the British official personnel there come under our ambassador. In am not aware that the U.A.R. asked for the evacuation of the British interests section of the Canadian embassy. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I felt that on this occasion we might have a statement from 
the Minister of Finance, notwithstanding the fact that he delivered himself of a budget speech the other night. There are a number of items that should be discussed because of their rather technical aspects. Perhaps the minister could give us some information. While I do not wish to get into a budget debate or anticipate the type of speech I would make in such a debate, there are a number of matters with regard to which we must ask the Minister of Finance for the views of the government and his predictions.
I turn first of all to the subject of interest rates. As we know, the Bank Act which was passed recently by this parliament has within the provisions of section 91, if my memory does not fail me, a rather intricate formula for the, shall we say, triggering-off of any ceiling on interest rates chargeable on some of the loans chartered banks may make. It is a sort of trigger formula for the removal of any ceiling on these interest rates.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
At the time the committee and this house were considering Bill No. C-222 last year there was a very clear indication by the minister and his officials that the interest rate of last year, in terms of the average rate for government short term loans, was declining. In effect, it was as a result of the minister's remarks that the committee decided to make an amendment to the act whereby the ceiling was fixed at 7| per cent for the balance of 1967. This was done because it was indicated that if interest rates declined as they had been doing over the course of the winter, some time next November the trigger in the Bank Act could operate, and it was deemed that there could be too sudden a change and therefore the rate should be phased out. But since then one has been hearing reports that a trough has been reached with regard to the decline in interest rates. As a matter of fact, the financial press has been replete with articles indicating that notwithstanding the relative freeing of money, interest rates are going into a reverse process and will probably go up as a result of strong demands for funds.
Does this mean that the trigger will not apply with regard to the Bank Act? I think the minister should now be in a position to tell us what he anticipates for the next half year with regard to interest rates in so far as they relate to the trigger formula under the Bank Act. I think the minister should also report in some detail on the developments under the Bank Act, the developments with regard to the Bank of Western Canada and
June 12, 1967

the Bank of British Columbia. We have also received notice now through the publishing of advertisements that there is another bank proposed for incorporation this year, the Bank of Alberta.
I ask the minister: is there anything in what some financial writers have said? Is there now too much competition? What are the views of the minister with regard to the developments under the Bank Act? I think this is an admirable time for the minister to give us his assessment of the situation. The new Bank Act has been in force only six or seven weeks, but already we have seen some significant developments with regard to types of savings accounts, the interest rate that is being paid to depositors in these bank accounts and the reaction of the near banks to them.
The next matter is related to the Bank Act but concerns a different subject. Is the minister in a position to tell us when the government intends to refer to the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs the regulations that were to be made with regard to interest disclosure? They may have been published in the Canada Gazette, but the Minister of Finance is not the one who files these details. This is done by the President of the Privy Council. As a matter of fact, it was only by a careful combing of all the Votes and Proceedings that I found that some weeks ago the President of the Privy Council had tabled the regulations made under the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act. It must be remembered that in this regard there was a very definite undertaking that the regulations would be sent to the finance, trade and economic affairs committee. I suggest this should not be done at the tail end of this session.
I think it is unfortunate that the committee did not have direct access to these regulations. Of course, the members of the committee can get the order in council and see what the regulations are, and I have already done so with regard to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, but the matter should be referred to the committee by way of resolution. The minister must bring in a resolution to refer these matters to the committee. I think the sooner this is done, the better off we will be. I hope to see such resolutions on the order paper within the next week with regard to both the Bank Act and the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act so that the rules and regulations will be turned over to the committee and we may consider them. We will not be able to attend to them before the
Supply-Finance
end of June, when parliament is scheduled to rise for a recess of an indefinite period, but at least we will have them before us and can talk to our friends and contacts within the banking system and the near banking system, who will be able to give us a professional assessment of these rules and regulations. We can then in the month of September, or earlier if that is to be the case, come back and be prepared to get down to work and discuss these matters rather more intelligently than would be the case if we were to arrive back here cold, as it were.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I make a special plea to the minister to see that his colleagues agree to these matters being put on the order paper and dealt with. As far as I am concerned and, I think, my colleague the hon. member for Perth-I cannot speak for my colleagues on the committee from other parties-we would be prepared to see such resolutions go through the house without debate in this instance so those regulations may be sent to the committee.
I trust that the minister will tell us something about a matter dealt with in numerous speeches which he has been making of late. The minister has a very good distribution service from his office and I receive pages and pages of speeches. They all have one central theme-the wisdom of Canada not doing anything to upset a continuing, strong flow of foreign funds for investment in this country. While the Minister of Finance has been making these speeches, ably assisted by the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development, other members of the cabinet have made speeches on a different theme. I do not know why we have not had a duel between the Minister of Forestry and Rural Development and the President of the Privy Council, because in other jurisdictions this is apparently how differences between members are sometimes settled. I suppose ours in Canada are really verbal duels.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
However, so far as ideas are concerned there is a head-on confrontation between the Minister of Finance and his associate, the minister of forestry on the one hand and the erstwhile minister of finance on the other. We know that a few weeks ago he really gave the old pail a solid kick and threatened to upset it when he spoke out on the subject of Viet Nam. Personally I find I cannot accept the view of the hon. member for Davenport concerning cabinet solidarity and his semantics regarding the expression of government poli-

June 12, 1967
Supply-Finance
cy and the expression of views or opinions. That is one luxury which the President of the Privy Council can no longer have now that he is back in the cabinet. Now he is off to the NATO ministers' conference in a related field of foreign affairs I fear we should tremble in dread of what ukases may come forth from him with regard to that aspect of our foreign affairs.
To return to the subject of foreign investment in Canada I point out that the speech from the throne dredged up as a prospective bride, for the fifth time I think, the Canada Development Corporation. I suppose it was originally in the thought of the then minister of finance who first propounded this idea that the Canada Development Corporation should be set up by the government of Canada. How was it going to operate? We were going to either buy back Canada or borrow back Canada. Here I am not using an original phrase; others have used it far more effectively than I can. We were going to go into debt financing rather than equity financing. However, this is not the time to argue in detail the pros and cons of equity versus debt financing, and I am certainly not going to argue ahead of time what I consider to be the potential tragedy in the introduction of the Canada Development Corporation. I can only point out that I do not think the Canadian people support this idea.
In a province as wealthy as the province of Alberta the Alberta Development Corporation was started. It was anticipated that $10 million would be raised in the first year, which is all right for a provincial jurisdiction. However, I doubt that they received subscriptions for $2 million. That is how far it went. In so far as the Canada Development Corporation is concerned, now that the Canada Pension Plan is siphoning off some $800 million a year from the private sector of investment into the public sector, there is to be even much less money available for investment in the Canada Development Corporation. Therefore I think the concurrent existence of the two, both competing for money, will place one more demand upon less and less dollars which are available to the taxpayers or the investors of the country. Notwithstanding the fact that the Canada Development Corporation has been referred to in the speech from the throne, I hope the Minister of Finance will see to it that this idea gets lost amidst the shuffle and press of parliamentary business and that it will ultimately be pigeonholed and there gather dust and remain merely an interesting idea which 
was put forward at one time by a man who had extremely nationalistic ideas in so far as Canada is concerned.
There is also another matter on which the minister may have made a brief statement. He will recall that when we were considering last year the estimates of the Department of Finance and also the Bank of Canada Act there was a good deal of discussion concerning the concrete decision by participants in the World Bank with regard to a new world monetary exchange unit. I believe that a conference was held not long ago and the minister reported to the house that he was disappointed that not as much progress had been made in this regard as he had hoped. I think he could elaborate on that subject so that we can see just where we are heading with regard to our world foreign exchange relationships.
There are indications of greater and greater pressure being put on the U.S. dollar, and certainly the results of last week's activities in the Middle East are likely to create a very serious potential problem for Great Britain, virtually a convertibility crisis in the making, because if a number of oil-rich Arab states which now hold tremendous sterling deposits in the United Kingdom suddenly get it in their minds that they will withdraw their funds and go off in a huff-I do not know where they would place their money-this would pose a very serious problem. As a matter of fact, we might see a further deterioration in the relationship between Great Britain and its erstwhile friends in the Middle East which would cause a blocking of sterling balances. This would upset the whole world pattern and prove the necessity for some form of agreement at least between the major countries of the world to ensure that a national unit shall not serve as the ultimate reserve for international exchange payments.
Several of my colleagues intend to speak in detail about the minister's estimates. There are one or two points that arose the other day when I attended a meeting of the committee on external affairs. As a matter of fact members of the committee were mystified at the tables which the director of the external aid branch produced with regard to the quantum of external aid supplied by Canada, and it was found that the figures he was using bore absolutely no relationship to the estimates as they appear in the blue book. The partial explanation was that the total of external aid was made up from a number of departments including, as the witness said, the Department of Finance. In this connection I would like to
June 12, 1967

know if there is some other source of external aid, apart from item 50, in the very general wording of these estimates which the Minister of Finance would consider as his contribution to external aid. If so, perhaps the minister could indicate it to the house.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Recently the minister issued some statements concerning small business loans made under the act of that name. One of these was dated June 2, 1967. I believe this act has been much maligned by being ignored by the public and the news media. As we know, this measure was brought into its modern dress and completely overhauled in 1959 or 1960, if my memory serves me right. I would not like to insist that the previous administration introduced that act because I have not been able to check that aspect, but certainly it was brought up to date about 1960.
It is very instructive to see how much money has been available to small businesses under this act. On June 2, 1967, the minister announced that loans totalling $3,590,997 were made to 401 borrowers under the Small Businesses Loans Act during the months January to March. The announcement does not say "inclusive" so I am not sure whether the minister was reporting for the first quarter of the calendar year 1967 or for only two months. At any rate, under this legislation the government may guarantee loans made by chartered banks for a wide range of business improvement purposes to small business enterprises engaged in manufacturing, wholesale and retail trade or in the service industries. A maximum of $25,000 may be lent to a borrower at any one time. Loans must be secured and may be repaid over periods of up to ten years. The maximum rate of interest is 5.5 per cent.
In my opinion, it is instructive to see how much money the banks have lent at 5.5 per cent over the past several years when money was allegedly so tight. The same situation applies, of course, to the Farm Improvement Loans Act, with regard to which I have a recent statement by the minister. In any event, I notice that according to the minister's statement the date of origin of the Small Businesses Loans Act was January, 1961, so I was not too far out when I suggested 1960. Since then, to the end of March, 1967, there have been 16,636 loans made for a total of $150,763,473.
I think this points up a salient fact, namely, that this was good legislation and the arrangements made thereunder with the banks and with the public have been working well.
Supply-Finance
Over 16,000 businesses, with a gross annual revenue of about $250,000 each, have benefited from this measure. Recently the maximum estimated gross annual revenue was raised to $500,000. These businessmen have been able to borrow $150 million at 5.5 per cent interest. I believe this is a clear indication that this was good legislation. I hope there will be a continuation of these facilities, that businessmen will avail themselves of them and that the banks will take advantage of the guarantee so the program will continue to be a satisfactory one.
The same remarks may be made in connection with the Farm Improvement Loans Act. In March of this year the Minister of Finance announced that 15,380 loans had been made for a total of $37,227,219 during the period October 1 to December 31, 1966. The total in 1966 was 85,553 loans for a total of $212,796,464 compared with 91,191 loans in 1965 for a total of $202,706,910. So here we have two heads of legislation, one for the small businessman and the other for the farmer for farm improvements. The Farm Improvement Loans Act is not designed to cover the purchase of farms because that comes under the Farm Credit Corporation. It is actually for the improvement of farms. When we look at these two measures we can see that the banks, with government co-operation, will provide loans at 5 per cent with the result that progress can be made.
I am not going to go into the details about the quantum of loans made under these acts. I merely point to them as examples of the fact that progress can be achieved with government co-operation without setting up government agencies. This is not what I want to do. I do not want to have the government acting as big brother. There is all too great a tendency toward this today. The government, along with business and individuals who may want to do some financing, can get an intelligent, workable program which does have good results.
There are a number of other people who want to speak on the estimates of the minister so I am going to conclude my remarks by saying that I hope the minister is not going to feel the estimates of his department are going to pass in a great hurry this year at the tail end of the session. I trust we will have a good discussion today. I do not believe we need to have an interminable discussion, but certainly we should have a reasoned and intelligent discussion. I am sure there will be other questions raised, but I should like the minister to give me answers to the points I have mentioned.

June 12, 1967

had perhaps missed an opportunity at the time of the regrettable collapse of one or two of these institutions, when I am sure that every provincial government was shaking in its shoes, in that he did not at that time suggest to them that the course of wisdom would be for them to insist that financial institutions licensed by the legislatures of the different provinces should voluntarily come under federal control and inspection.
I had the feeling at that time that every provincial government would have realized that this was the lifeline of safety in face of the very serious developments which were taking place within the financial institutions of the different provinces. I am quite sure the minister is fully aware that that was the psychological moment to do it and that he was deterred from doing it for fear of adverse reactions from one particular province. I think that federal governments will have to get over their continual phobia about the possibility of reactions from that province if we are going to advance as a nation.
I should like to say a word or two about another of those ticklish questions which came before the committee, and that is the position of the Mercantile Bank of Canada. I raised the matter with the minister not long ago in the house on the basis of an article which appeared in the Executive magazine which, while it was not conclusive, suggested to me that Mr. Rockefeller and his associates are planning to do precisely what I suggested they might do when the motion which I seconded was introduced in the committee to give the bank a five year period in which to expand their operations and make their shares attractive to Canadian investors. I had an uneasy feeling at that time, despite the blandishments of the hon. member for Verdun, that Mr. Rockefeller and his associates might be preparing to play a game of Russian roulette with the minister and would keep telling him that the time is not now propitious to put their shares on the market, that they would finally come up against the five year limit and would point out that it was still not propitious, and then would say to the minister: "What are you going to do now? Are you going to confine us to the 20 to one ratio or are you going to allow us to go on expanding in defiance of your legislation?"
I should like to be sure that the minister is keeping a very sharp eye on this situation. I confess that my interest is largely because of the history and the record of this financial group in the United States of America and its 27053-90
Supply-Finance
operations outside that country, which lead me to the conclusion that while there may perhaps be a case to be made out for permitting a foreign bank to enter the Canadian business community, this is not a group that I should like to see in Canada. I say that because their record in other countries renders them, to my mind, somewhat suspect of being rather ruthless, rather concerned for their own interests to the neglect of the interests of the host country.
I too, like the hon. member for Edmonton West, was interested in the minister's remarks about the necessity to maintain the inflow of United States capital. I noticed that at least in one speech he based his anxiety that the flow should continue on the need to have capital to expand the Canadian economy. If one looks at it in one way I suppose that is a reasonable and correct estimate, but actually I am sure the minister knows there has been almost no net inflow of United States capital for development in Canada for some time. What we do have is an inflow of capital which balances the now rapidly increasing outflow. In fact, we need more in order to pay for the loss of previous investment. The bulk of the expansion of the Canadian economy in non-Canadian hands takes place on the basis of the retained earnings of existing subsidiaries of foreign corporations. Eventually I think the minister will have to face up to this problem and determine whether or not we are being fair to the people of Canada by allowing this continual expansion on the basis of funds earned in Canada from the work of Canadians to result in expansion of foreign holdings in our economy.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I have wondered whether the minister has considered the possibility of fiscal measures that would make it a little less attractive to plow back such an enormous volume of retained earnings, that would make it a little less attractive to have such a large body of retained earnings. After all, when we find that 70 per cent-perhaps it is over 70 per cent now-of capital for new investment comes from internally generated savings we can see that this is a most serious matter.
The hon. member for Edmonton West had some acid comments about the Canada Development Corporation. I will not make acid comments about it until I find out what type of beast it will be. It has had a number of sea changes and it may have some more. I can see that such a corporation might be

June 12, 1967
Supp ly-Finance
extremely useful, not to buy back foreign-owned holdings in Canada which, to be fair, I frankly believe is an imbecility, but to act as a means of expanding the Canadian economy in Canadian hands so that the proportion of foreign-owned holdings in Canada will decline in relation to the whole.
I can see where the Canada Development Corporation could be a very valuable institution into which to pool a large part of the capital required for our expansion.
The hon. member for Edmonton West had some scathing comments, or, to use another word, some deplorable comments to make about the effect of the Canada Pension Plan and that it drained so much money from the private sector into public hands. No one would expect me to sympathize with the hon. member on that score. I wish at this time to reiterate a proposal that I have made a number of times in the house. I hope that the Minister of Finance at some time will see that my proposal is not so much for a publicly owned banking complex as something that it would be sensible for a harassed minister of finance to follow. My proposal is that we extend the operations of the Canada Pension Plan and that we offer the Canadian people a series of options. I do not see why we should allow private groups-and we are licensing more and more of them every session of parliament-to take control of the savings of the Canadian people and to do with those savings what they will. Indeed, if the minister is concerned about continuing the flow of United States capital to balance the outflow and to produce investments he will keep a careful eye on the investment dollars of life insurance companies in Canada, both Canadian and foreign owned, and he will find, interestingly enough, that there is nothing to choose between them in their investment policies.
Canadian and foreign owned life insurance companies invest up to 50 per cent of their total investments outside Canada and not in the development of this country. That is a compelling argument for expanding the operations of the Canada Pension Plan in such a manner that it will attract the vast bulk of the savings which now go into private hands, and over which, as investment funds, we have no control.
I, too, wish to say a word or two about the reform of the international monetary system. First, I wish to pay tribute to those officials of the Bank of Canada who have worked extremely hard in presenting Canada's view at

international conferences on this matter-regrettably, without too much success-and I express the hope that before long we shall persuade the other trading nations of the world of the necessity of establishing a new and additional unit of international exchange; I hope that we shall not be frightened by the possible implications of such a move that was suggested first, I think, by the prominent economist, John Maynard Keynes. I think that it was the late Lord Keynes who said, after he had introduced his idea of Bancor, that if it were adopted it would be the first step toward global administration.
He should have kept his mouth shut, because I am sure his suggestion frightened many people off at that time, just as I am sure the same idea frightens them today. Nevertheless, so far as I am concerned, this is an added argument in favour of a reformed international monetary system. If exchange positions have been acute up to now-and I know that opinions vary on this topic-I think we can all be sure that they will become increasingly acute as the United States economy suffers from increasingly severe strains owing to its military commitments in southeast Asia. The United States strains will bring an almost unbearable load to the international monetary system and methods of exchange as they now exist.
I was greatly heartened to see that in Canada we have extremely competent people in the Bank of Canada who are fully aware of these problems and are advancing our ideas in the world. I hope that the minister and the Government of Canada presses these ideas as decisively as possible.
The reform of the international monetary system is essential, not merely to deal with the present volume of world trade, but, more importantly, to solve the problems of the present century in promoting the development of the undeveloped countries of the world and to enable their populations to enter the twentieth century. That can be made possible only by the technological revolution of our times. Nothing must be allowed to stand in the way of that development. It is not a matter of charity, philanthropy or humanitarianism; it is a matter of survival. If Canada and the other members of the affluent world are not prepared to grapple with this problem of developing the undeveloped countries, then humanity will be in a precarious way. One of the tools with which we must work is a modernized international monetary system of exchange.
June 12, 1967

With those words I share with the hon. member for Edmonton West the hope that the minister, before we are finished this debate, may give us his ideas on these and other points which I am sure he has in his mind.

subsubtopic: ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to bring a few points to the attention of the Minister of Finance. I criticize the failure to provide sufficient funds in the estimates in those areas where money is so sorely needed. Also, I wish to compliment the minister for removing the sales tax on drugs, something which I and other members of the house have advocated for many years. That was a worth-while step.
I am interested to know what the minister intends to do with respect to the drug industry as an industry. I shall mention only a few firms. In this country we have old firms such as Ayerst, McKenna & Harrison, Limited which produces natural hormones for the production of estrogen and other valuable drugs as well. Such firms produce drugs which are of great benefit to Canada and other countries. The industry also employs many men who do research that is beneficial to agriculture. Especially useful is that research that has to do with mares for the production of estrogen.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
I refer also to the Warner-Lambert firm, a multimillion dollar outfit that came to Toronto and is doing medical research, research into the production of drugs, which we have not got at present, and research in many fields which if it was not done would be a great potential loss. I also want to draw to the attention of the minister that this firm brought in Dr. Lumb, a British scientist doing research in the United States, which is one instance of a reverse brain drain. They were able to set up in Toronto a multimillion dollar investment in plant and equipment. I am also going to mention Smith, Kline and French. They have invested over $2 million in the Montreal area where they are conducting an extensive research program.
What is the intention of the government? Is it to remove all the advantages of this drug research or do they propose, as they propose in industry, to subsidize all those industries in Canada which find it difficult to meet competition from abroad? I think these are the questions that the Minister of Finance must ask himself, because the drug industry in Canada is far too important to write off with a shrug saying that cheap drugs are the only advantage we require in this country. We have to think of the research done and the
Supply-Finance
scientists and other people who are trained and developed in Canada, as well as employment. Has this investigation been done?
I want to deal also with the health resources fund from the point of view that today we are tremendously short of doctors. Three years ago I drew this problem to the attention of the hon. member for Davenport, then minister of finance, and said the government should be getting ready to provide finances to run medical schools during the summer. This government brought in the medicare legislation two years before it goes into effect. I do not blame the Minister of Finance for the delay because he said there were certain financial problems involved, but I am saying that he said: Come what may we are going to bring it on July 1, 1968. I want to ask him what provision has been made to service the medicare contracts that they propose giving to the Canadian people. Are they going to cheat them and say they cannot possibly fulfil them because they have done nothing to guarantee there will be the number of doctors required to fulfil the demands of medicare across this country?
I have urged him to do this and newspapers have urged him to do it. There have been half a dozen editorials such as one in the Toronto Star a couple of weeks ago urging the government to supply the funds for summer terms in medical schools. This is an easy thing to do. It is not expensive. All you have to do is have the medical students who are taking a six year course at Queen's or at the University of Toronto take summer courses and you will create doctors in four years. This would mean an increase of one and a half times in the number of doctors graduating. This would in some measure meet the requirement for doctors set out in the Hall commission report.
Some may say, why was it not done? The biggest problem, according to what I have been told by people in the know or who should be in the know, is that funds would have to be provided to enable these medical students to go to school in the summer and not have to go out to work. The money could be made available through loans because once they graduate they are able to earn the money to repay any advances. But over and above that you will not be cheating the Canadian taxpayer out of something he is entitled to receive and for which he will be paying the bill under medicare.
Just in case the minister thinks I am rather hot on this point I want to draw his attention to an article by Dr. K. C. Thomson, past

June 12, 1967
Supply-Finance
president of the Canadian Medical Association. He was describing the health resources fund of $500 million. This fund which was announced with glowing praise was described as a source of moneys to provide Canada with health education facilities. The need had been emphasized earlier by the Hall commission as a requirement to be met before Canada introduced any medical health insurance scheme whatever.
The minister said it is coming on July 1, 1968, without proper preparation. That is the only conclusion one can draw. The Hall report called for a great increase in doctors, nurses, technicians and all the personnel required for adequate medical care before medicare was instituted. Doctor Thomson goes on to say it is all right to build these structures if the provinces can match the grants dollar for dollar. Again I want to say to the minister that taxes went up 14 per cent federally last year. Some of us criticized him for that. I did not criticize him on that occasion. But at the same time provincial taxes across Canada went up by 25 per cent. I know he wants to be fair. With these increases, how in the world can the provincial governments go ahead and match the health resources fund dollar for dollar unless they are among the wealthiest provinces in Canada? I do not believe any of them can do it.
But after the minister has done that and has provided for the buildings, what about the staff facilities? What is the use of putting $500 million into buildings if we have not got the personnel to operate them? It comes back to the point that we are not providing the funds to do it. Again I quote this medical research report. It states that medical research needs a minimum of $56 million during 1967-68. For 1967-68, government grants total $25 million or less than half the amount prescribed in the report. This is not good enough. I tell you, Mr. Chairman, that there is a crisis in the medical profession. Town after town in Canada is without doctors. I drove through one the other night which the doctor had left just the other day. In the town of Wingham two of the four doctors have pulled out and of the two who remain one is suffering from a heart condition and the other is getting along in years. There is a hospital in that town. Who will serve the public there? Who will do the night calls?
I am not blaming the federal government entirely because this is also a provincial affair but I come back to the point that the federal
[Mr. Rynard.l
government is not pulling its weight in providing the necessary funds so that the provinces can discharge their responsibilities. This is the point I am making. I want to read again from Dr. Thomson's report and put it on the record that we cannot afford to forget research. Canada has a brilliant record. He points out that the American Medical Association has quoted the Economic Council of Canada as the authority for saying that 2,000 graduate physicians and surgeons left Canada in the decade 1953-1963.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
That is over a ten year period and it means 200 physicians per year. At present it costs $50,000 to graduate a doctor. I do not have to belabour the economics of that because the minister should be smarter than I am in this field. Further, many of those who go to the United States are doing research work there.
We in Canada have had a spectacular record in research. It was in Canada that insulin was discovered by Banting and Best. Look at the boon to diabetics that was and money it has brought in on patent rights. We had Collp with the isolation of hormones from the parathyroid, the pituitary and the placenta, the discovery and introduction of anti-coagulants, major surgical achievements in epilepsy, and revascularization of the heart vessels. Look at Montreal, at Vineberg and the work he did. Other Canadian successes have been the use of hypothermia in surgery, cyclopropane in anesthesia, and the identification of the sex chromatin. I could continue with the list.
The Canadian Medical Association reports on the brain drain and hopes that it may be stemmed or even reversed. Dr. Thomson and his associates hope so. Just in case the minister might think I am over zealous I wish to quote an article which appeared in the Oshawa Times on June 5, 1967. It reads:
The shortage of medical men in Ontario is a problem of growing and serious proportions.
And this applies across Canada.
Back in 1964 anxiety over the situation was expressed by the Hall Royal Commission on health services . ..
The four medical schools of Ontario have been graduating 300 doctors every year since the second world war. In the same period the population has almost doubled.
According to Dr. John Evans, dean of the medical faculty at McMaster University, the profession is fighting a "losing battle" in trying to supply new doctors.
I want the minister to pay particular attention to that because he is the one who finally
June 12, 1967

put the stamp on medicare which is to come into force on July 1, 1968, no matter what happens. I continue the quotation:
A start has been made. At Queen's, Toronto, Western and Ottawa, medical schools are being expanded. A new medical school at McMaster will open in two years.
But Dr. Evans claims that this is not enough. He suggests that the medical course should be shortened.
I am not an expert on the training of doctors and I am sure the Minister of Finance is not either, but I believe we can shorten the present course to four years by making it a continuous course and dividing it into three semesters. By doing that we would produce as many doctors in four years as it is presently taking us six years.
It now takes a medical student seven years after grade 13 before he can qualify for practice. Another two or three years must pass before he can specialize.
Now comes the point that I want the minister to consider:
If the government underwrote medical education completely, it would not be necessary for students to take four months off in the summer to earn money to continue, the Kingston Whig Standard comments.
In passing I would point out that the Minister of National Revenue comes from Kingston where Queen's University is situated.
Under a new system training could go on all year. Also, as is being shown at Queen's, the course can be safely shortened by eliminating nonessentials. McMaster plans to cut a year off the four years of medical studies by carrying on all year.
It would not be a loss to Canada if the government underwrote medical education completely. The money could be given as loans to students and every nickel would be paid back. Such a scheme would guarantee more doctors and perhaps stop some of the brain drain to the United States.
Another thing I want to point out to the minister is that it is my understanding that at present we have fewer interns in Canadian hospitals than we have had at any time during the last five years. At the same time there is more outpatient care at our hospitals. Outpatient care is increasing at the rate of about 15 per cent per year but the hospitals are understaffed. I ask the minister, what does he propose to do about this? He is the one who put the stamp of approval on the medicare bill which is to come into operation on July 1 next year.
I am not being critical of the minister. I am not being critical of anybody. I am merely
Supply-Finance
trying to direct the attention of hon. members to a very serious situation. Every dean of medicine across Canada can testify to the crisis we find ourselves in today, but the government sits here, not providing the funds to do the things that are necessary in order to graduate the doctors that are needed. The situation is so bad that if a person moves to another town and does not know a doctor there or is not recommended to one the only place he can get attention is in the emergency department of a hospital. This is because all doctors are busy and overworked.
I warn the minister that a cracking point comes, and the cracking point in this case comes when governments make a second class profession of the medical profession because of their lack of support. I appeal to the Minister of Finance to provide the funds necessary to allow medical schools to operate during the summer. He should also provide funds for teaching and facilities in the new medical centres which are to be built whenever the provinces find themselves in a position to match dollar for dollar the funds granted by the federal government.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I was raised in a somewhat Calvinistic atmosphere in my home. I was always told by my father and mother that I should never buy anything unless I had the cash to pay for it. I have tried to practice that throughout my life. They also told me that if I denied myself in order to save money to buy the things I wanted, I would get more happiness from those things than if I went into debt to get them. So, Mr. Chairman, although I am one of the most progressive members of this group I am somewhat influenced by my home environment when I approach questions of finance.
I have always believed that the people of Canada are entitled to all the programs they are willing to support but that nothing is free. People are entitled to all the programs they want if they are willing to support the taxes required to pay for the programs. The money has to be taken from some one. No government can give anything in the way of services or funds to any group of person without taking it from some other group or person in our society. We have to realize the significance of that.
First, Mr. Chairman, I want to say I appreciate the minister's personal attention to any problems I have brought to his notice. I might say that my constituents also appreciate receiving copies of his letters which show

June 12, 1967
Supply

Finance
that he has replied in person to the problems they brought to my attention and that I later brought to his notice.
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
Let me say that I was glad to hear that the competent officials of the Bank of Canada are working to promote international monetary reform. I think this is urgently necessary in the first instance if we are going to have complete national control of our own finances and independence in that direction, and also if we are to accept our global responsibilities to the underdeveloped countries which require our assistance on a logical, long-term and sound basis.
Once again let me bring to the minister's attention that I am one of those who believe that the Bank of Canada can be used to provide the social capital required by federal, provincial and municipal governments and that we should utilize the Bank of Canada for that purpose. I understand there are certain steps being taken in this direction but that nothing very much has been done to date. When I look at our debt charges, which I judge to be over $127 million per year, I think this is more than ever necessary.
I am not going to repeat the things I said the last time I spoke on this subject, but I should like to bring to the minister's attention some interesting correspondence from a certain gentleman writing on behalf of the Social Credit federal election association. Fancy me quoting them. The letter is from the honorary secretary, Mr. George Howland, 361 Vancouver Avenue, Nanaimo, British Columbia. The correspondence reads as follows:
A reduction or cancellation of the 8 per cent of bank deposits gives a golden opportunity to provide for short term interest free loans to he made available.
The bank should not have so valuable a proposal handed to them free of charge, so to speak.
Part of the extra dollars which would come within their grasp should be made, by compulsion, available to those provinces asking for interest free loans, when they can back their requests with satisfactory evidence that they could supply as cover, bonds saleable on a par with other gilt-edged securities.
It is an indisputable fact that Mr. Robert Thompson, leader of the Social Credit party and Mr. T. Douglas, leader of the New Democratic Party are 100 per cent in favour of interest free loans; letters from them are evidence of this. If the Creditistes and either the Liberal or Conservative leaders also favour such loans, now is the time for action.
Today we are having a revision of the Bank Act; to lose this opportunity might mean many years wait for another one.

speechtext: Has the hon. member converted his fellow N.D.P. members?

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE

speechtext:
Yes, and I shall read a letter which will show that I am right on the beam. This correspondence was sent to my leader who replied on July 2, 1965. I want to place his letter in reply on the record. It is addressed to Mr. George Howland and states:
Dear Mr. Howland:
Thank you very much for your letter of June 25 and for enclosing the leaflet advocating interest free loans to provincial governments and local government bodies.
This is in keeping with the program of the New Democratic Party. Indeed, I think we must go further and have the federal government make grants for at least 50 per cent of the expenditures for schools, hospitals, etc. in areas which require such assistance.
Thanks again for writing me in this connection and kindest personal regards.
Yours sincerely,
T. C. Douglas.
I hope the minister will not ask any more questions as to whether I am dealing with party policy, because this is the best evidence I could possibly give of my leader's support for the programs I have been urging upon the Bank of Canada from time to time. A great deal could be done in this direction because these loans would be made on our ability to repay, on our resources and industrial structure, as well as on the capacity of the Canadian people to produce. Why should we not use the Bank of Canada to develop our country in the way I suggest?
I was very interested in the remarks of the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowiehan-The Islands regarding the accumulating Canadian pension fund capital. Surely that could be used in conjunction with action on the part of the Bank of Canada to promote public and private investment in this country. Surely there are plenty of opportunities for this money to be used on a sound and satisfactory basis.
In addition we have the Industrial Development Bank which provides capital for smaller private industries. It has been very useful to several small industries in my own constituency which required assistance at a certain time. As a result of that assistance these industries were established, have become successful and have grown.
I believe there has been a failure in recognizing the great opportunities for the development of the credit union movement in this country as it relates to the mobilization of the savings of the working people. I called the
June 12, 1957

first meeting for this purpose in my constituency when I was in the provincial house and helped organize the credit union in Trail. At the time this credit union was organized there were six or seven people present and it was obvious that many of the workers did not feel the working man could handle his own money properly. It may be of interest to note that at the present time in the constituency of Kootenay West there is over $15 million in the capital of credit unions. They provide loans to working people in respect of consumer goods as well as an opportunity for investment. These credit unions are now supplying money to road contractors and people of that sort, and did so particularly at a time when they were unable to obtain money from the banks. The federal and provincial governments could do a lot more to promote and stimulate this movement.
What we need at this time is a national credit union act. This is particularly true because these credit unions are operating as a result of the participation of those Canadians concerned. This provides a tremendous opportunity for the mobilization of a very large amount of capital which can be used for consumer loans, investment and in the development of small local industries in the areas where the credit unions are organized. When the minister replies I hope he will indicate the government's intention in respect of a national credit union act. Let me emphasize the fact that there is tremendous opportunity in this field and tremendous enthusiasm on the part of those groups who utilize these credit unions and support them.
I should also like to ask the minister what progress has been made in the study of charitable donations. Chambers of commerce, farmers organizations and other groups have throughout the years made certain representations in connection with exemptions for donations to charitable organizations. I am in favour of providing an exemption if the donations are actually made to charitable organizations and not to organizations masquerading as such.
[DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
When the minister replies I hope he will have something to say in this regard, and I hope he will give some further consideration to those individuals who are holders of perpetual bonds. I have received quite a lot of correspondence about this matter, as I am sure other members have, and I have always felt that these people were not being treated fairly in respect of the small amounts they
Supply-Finance
hold. I think consideration could be given to their circumstances, especially where they bought these bonds having in mind that they would be something to fall back on when they reached retirement age. The persons I hear from generally are those who have a number of these bonds and who expected the interest would be available and would be useful at a time when they were no longer working. I do urge further consideration of this problem.
I had several other questions to bring to the attention of the minister. I have written him about these matters and he has replied promptly and in detail. I think consideration should be given to the sort of overlapping between federal and provincial responsibility in connection with certain financial questions, acceptance corporations and things of that sort. It is a very foggy area at the present time and should be more clearly defined.
That is all I have to say at this moment. I certainly look forward to hearing what the minister intends to do about the several matters I have brought to his attention. Before I sit down may I say I can almost feel that I have made him a convert to my philosophy with respect to the issuing of loans by the Bank of Canada to all governments that require them for investment in social capital.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I ought to say a few words about the estimates of the Department of Finance. I regret that the former minister of finance, now President of the Privy Council, is not here to give the house the benefit of his philosophy, which for some reason seems not to be accepted by the present minister and others of the cabinet. But the Minister of Finance's loss is NATO's gain.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE

speechtext:
Totally unacquainted with international affairs, the President of the Privy Council left Canada a couple of days ago to accompany the Secretary of State for External Affairs to deal with problems of NATO. This is a matter of very considerable importance when one considers the expenditures in respect of foreign affairs. Whether there is any significance in the fact that he is now abroad, having expressed the view that NATO should be abolished, will be an interesting study during the days ahead.
Why did the former minister of finance depart this country at a time when his views would have been so helpful, namely, when the estimates of the Minister of Finance are before the committee? The President of the Privy Council has gone abroad to deal with

June 12, 1967
Supply-Finance
international affairs, a subject he has shown no capacity to understand up to the present time. Is it a fact that having joined the entourage for NATO is the first indication by the government that his views are now being accepted and that NATO, at a time when it should be strengthened, faces the danger of being weakened if the philosophy of the former minister of finance is accepted? These things occur to those who endeavour to look at what is called in certain circles the spectrum created by a government that goes every direction on every subject and is always able to say that some minister has taken a position contrary to that followed by the others.
In this centennial year the Minister of Finance has much to boast about. It begins to look as though he will be the Minister of Finance with the greatest deficit in Canada's peacetime history. It looks as though we will have a billion dollar deficit unless there is an assiduous application of paring down. Up to the present time this government has shown no sign of believing in the necessity of that. The Minister of Finance is able to boast in centennial year that he has introduced the heaviest taxation in Canada's history. During his period of office he has increased taxation in several fields to the extent of hundreds of millions of dollars. He is able to boast in centennial year that under his administration the highest cost of living in all history has been attained.
These things are deserving of mention, particularly when it is realized that the minister belongs to that group that had all the answers to all the problems in 1963. At that time, when Canada was spending something over $6 billion, it was a frightful situation for this nation. This year it will be at least $400 million more.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE

speechtext: Four billion dollars more.

subtopic: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE

speechtext:
Yes, $4 billion more. After all, as Mr. Howe said, "What's a million, anyhow?" The only difference between Mr. Howe and this government is that they have substituted "billion" for "million".
I do not wish to deal with the budget directly at this time, but I am sure, Mr. Chairman, you will allow me to say that while everybody commends the removal of the tax on drugs it is particularly appropriate, having regard to the things I mentioned a moment ago-the prospective billion dollar deficit, the highest taxes in Canadian history and the highest cost of living in Canadian history-that aspirin will now be cheaper.

This will no doubt assist Canadians as a whole to suffer less pain. Again I say I do not want to deal with the budget because it will be dealt with later. In fact there was no budget; therefore there can be no infraction of the rules in simply referring to that document.
I wish to deal with the fiscal payments to the provinces. There, too, the great men who now sit opposite had all the answers. They would bring about a fiscal system that would help the provinces, and deny any possibility of injustice or unfairness. On page 149 of the present estimates the statutory payments to the provinces are listed in accordance with the recent fiscal arrangements. During our period of office we would not have had a deficit in any year, I think, had it not been for the increased payments that we made to the provinces in order to assist them to discharge their jurisdictional authority and responsibility.

In 1958 we entered into new agreements. We did not have to enter into new agreements; the agreements still had four years to run. We entered into new agreements because we realized that the provinces could not carry out the responsibilities set out in the British North America Act. We helped them. We gave new hope to the Atlantic provinces. We made it easier for the people of the maritimes to walk as Canadians, upright and without fear. The hon. member for Vic-toria-Carleton, who at that time was premier of New Brunswick, knows it well. Now what has happened? The government has been tinkering with this problem, failing to face up to it.
The figures relating to the distribution of increases in 1967-68 over the previous year give an indication that there is something radically wrong with the fiscal policies, of this government. In 1967-68 Newfoundland is to receive $71 million compared with $47 million in the previous year. Prince Edward Island receives $14.2 million compared with $10.4 million. Nova Scotia receives $79.3 million compared with $50.8 million. New Brunswick receives $70.6 million compared with $46.4 million. Even with these increases the provinces cannot carry out their responsibilities.
Quebec receives $280.5 million compared with $158.7 million in the previous year. Ontario will receive in 1967-68 $18.8 million and in the previous year it received $17.1
June 12, 1967

million. I will leave it to the Ontario members to devote themselves to the study of the figures that I place before the committee.
I come to western Canada. Manitoba receives $34.2 million compared with $30.7 million. Saskatchewan was forgotten. It is to receive this year $28.9 million compared with $35.4 million, a substantial reduction of some $6.5 million. Alberta will receive the same sum as it did the previous year. Why has there been such a reduction in the sum given to Saskatchewan? What is the variety of abstruse mathematical calculation performed in the recesses of the Department of Finance? Why was this done. All the mathematical formulae that can be produced, all the juggling that the minister can do, cannot explain the unfairness to the province of Saskatchewan. I would be the last to suggest that there were any political connotations or that the province is being penalized to any extent because of the last federal election. But why is there such a situation? Am I unfair in this criticism?
Anyone who thinks so should hear what the premier of Saskatchewan has to say. He knows this government. He is fully acquainted with the Minister of Finance, and his views are of a nature that I would not want to repeat them in the House of Commons lest the government blush with shame. Somewhere in this equation there is an X factor. Is the X factor related to the voting record? These are questions that naturally arise. The minister cannot say that the province wanted it this way because he will recall his hurried trip to Toronto to meet the premier of Saskatchewan. That was not a get-together for social purposes. What explanation did the minister advance to the premier of Saskatchewan for having knocked down the $35 million to approximately $29 million? These are things which we would like to hear about from the minister.
The situation today in dominion-provincial fiscal relations is far removed from the concept that the Fathers of Confederation had in mind and also far removed from the principles that activated the Mackenzie King and St. Laurent administrators in their day. No glib response can answer the charge that this government has failed the provinces. There is no question about it. It is because it has failed the provinces that it refuses to convene a dominion-provincial conference on the subject of confederation. We have asked for it. The Canadian people are in a mood to bring about the necessary agreements on the constitution 27053-91
Supply-Finance
in keeping with the experience of 100 years, agreements which will assure the provinces that they will be able to carry out their responsibilities.
We were told for about a year and a half the government could not act. The minister said he could not do anything because the Carter commission had not reported. When the Carter commission did report the alibi was that they had to examine the recommendations very carefully. That is true and I can understand it. Now consideration is to be postponed again. There is to be another meeting as mentioned today by the Prime Minister. It is just simple eyewash on the part of the government to pretend that it intends to do something about the Carter recommendations while at the same time it does everything it can to postpone and procrastinate in anticipation hopefully of not having to do anything. What is going to be done? This cannot go on. Confederation cannot live with the day to day and year to year handouts which this government perpetuates.
There will have to be acceptance of the principle that in certain fields the provinces have rights of taxation, otherwise we will build up within this nation concepts far removed from the determination of the Fathers of Confederation. I might deal with this later after the minister gives an answer to the questions that have been asked.
I come to a matter of interest not only to Canada but to western Canada in particular. What has happened to the Bank of Western Canada? It was not very long ago that Sinclair Stevens and his group, B.I.F. and all the subsidiaries which he had gathered together, were going to operate the bank. This was the new wizard of finance with all the ideas. Trust companies were absorbed and included in B.I.F. He decided he should go into the banking field. One can understand why he thought action was necessary. I should have paid a further tribute to the minister. He is the minister who, in this confederation year, has produced the highest interest rates. Everybody is being mulcted under this government. We have the highest taxes, highest interest rates and highest cost of living.

cost of drugs and for announcing the date on which the federal sales tax on drugs will be eliminated. The second reason for taking part in this debate on the estimates of the Department of Finance is to express my appreciation for all this government has done to assist municipalities in relieving the local unemployment problem and providing more public services. Similar legislation, Mr. Chairman, was enacted under the Kennedy administration in the United States. I hope it will be possible to have such legislation introduced in our parliament.

Mr. Chairman, I have a very simple request to make of the minister and perhaps he could reply to it when he replies to the other requests that have been made. I want to raise a problem in connection with the working mother who is a widow, has children and perforce has to engage a babysitter to look after her children while she earns their keep. I think that this problem is fairly common in different parts of Canada, and it is one I should like to see tackeld by the Department of Finance through the budgetary laws of the country to the end that such people may be given some relief. For a few hours of the day they are required to hire a babysitter for their children, and part of what they earn is spent on this purpose.
When a man suffers bereavement through the loss of his wife certain provisions in the income tax law give him relief. However, this problem has been drawn to my attention by various widows in the Halifax area. I realize that the widows in the rest of Canada belong to the hon. member for Kootenay West but there are a number who are pleased to present their problems to me. I believe that the problem is a substantial one with which parliament should come to grips. Such expenditure is surely a legitimate expense that should be deductible from gross income.
