Mr. Chairman, may I open my remarks by saying that I am perhaps one of the few members of the House of Commons who would be quick to tell the Minister of Finance that he is not an expert on financial matters. I assure the minister that when I study company and bank balances, credits and debits, appreciation and depreciation, income tax, corporation tax payments and reserves for same, quite honestly I become completely confused. I am one-I think there are many more like me in this house-who, when I receive my cheque at the end of the month and deposit it in the bank, pay my bills and anxiously look forward to my next month's cheque hoping that what I have left will last

June 12, 1967
Supply-Finance
till that time. Therefore in making my remarks this evening I am not speaking as an expert on finances in any way.
There is one phase of financial investment about which I hope the minister will give an explanation to a great many people in the country. I refer to those in the aged group who have only a little money, those typically who have $1,000, $3,000, $5,000 or perhaps $10,000. Thousands of people in Canada who have but little money and do not want to lose it honestly believe that the finest guaranteed investment they can make is in federal government bonds. This is almost axiomatic in the thinking of people with small savings, with only so many years ahead of them, who want to know that they are going to be paid interest on their investment and, in particular, will never lose their capital. In addition, Mr. Chairman, there are certain types of trust, such as education trusts, which by law can invest only in government bonds or, on occasion, in first mortgages.
What has been the experience of these people to whom I refer? Over the months I have received letter after letter from people who have invested their money to provide for themselves in their declining years. However, sometimes an emergency arises and they have to sell their investments. What happens to those who invest in government bonds? They find themselves in a paradoxical situation financially that I confess I do not understand. They sell their government bonds sometimes at heavy loss on their capital investment. I understand the reason for this is the money market, and that when you invest money you do so on the understanding that you hold your security until maturity date. I once had an experience, not a personal one, with an education trust where money was suddenly required and I believe the trust lost about $8 of its capital investment on each $100 bond purchased.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
The only point I am trying to make is that there are thousands of people who trust the federal government and who are not familiar with the complexities and intricacies of finance and the effect of the money market on government bonds. As I say, these people trust the federal government and trust investment in federal bonds. I have recently been advised that such people cannot sell their bonds without suffering a capital loss. It is true that they can borrow money from the bank on the security of their government

bonds but then they suffer a loss because of the interest they have to pay. The loss through interest payments is not as great perhaps as the loss they would suffer by the sale of their capital investments.
Perhaps my presentation is needlessly complex, but this question concerns thousands of Canadians. They have put their trust in the federal government and in federal bonds. Can the minister say what action people ought to take when they wish to reclaim some of their money? What are they to do if they are not to lose part of their capital and retain their trust in government bonds? The government has needed money and has entered the world financial market. The people of our country have invested in government bonds but when they are in dire need of money and wish to sell their bonds they lose on their capital investment.
I hope that the minister understands the point I am trying to raise because I do not know how else to put it. I have received many letters asking that the problem I have referred to be corrected. Those buying government bonds are real Canadians who by thrift have saved their money and have invested it in Canada. They are people who, when they are in dire need, find that the Canadian government lets them down and allows them to lose money on the capital they have invested in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I want to add to what has already been said about making it possible for women working outside the home to deduct the expenses of babysitters or housekeepers from their income tax returns. They should be able to make a deduction for those expenses in the same way as businessmen deduct for business expenses. It is necessary that this be done.
Great numbers of women working outside the home are the sole support of their families and if their families are not to be neglected they must have housekeeping or babysitting services during working hours. There is no provision in any thoroughgoing way for housewives to deduct these expenses at the present time. We also find that in many families the husband is a widower and has to work and provide housekeeping services for his family. It is important that children should not be allowed to run at large or be without proper housekeeping services. Such expenses also ought to be deductible.
Many women who work outside the home cannot possibly afford from their wages or salaries the expenses of babysitters. In certain countries such as the United States and the United Kingdom the tax position for married women is quite favourable. Here I am thinking about the way married women are permitted to make deductions for their expenses from income tax. For example, in the United States a working wife can deduct up to $900 for child care expenses when there are two or more children, or $600 for one child. The stipulations are that the child be not more than 12 years old and that the joint income of the parents not exceed $6,000.
In the United Kingdom preference is given to working married women. They get a single person's tax free allowance for earnings, in addition to the husband benefiting from the married man's allowance which is nearly double the single person's.
Supply-Finance
The tax structures in a few countries, on the other hand, appear to be intended to discourage the wives of all but the neediest of husbands from employment. In the Netherlands, for example, a married woman's earnings are taxed 15 per cent if she is not the breadwinner.
My remarks at this time are directed particularly to the plight of the nursing profession. It is essential that married women who are nursing be able to deduct the expenses of housekeeping services. For married nurses, who represent 60 per cent of all nurses employed full time, the present tax policies must be frustrating, costly, and discouraging. That these nurses continue to work in spite of them is proof of their desire to remain active in the profession.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
For the 19,781 married nurses listed as "not employed in nursing" in 1965 the present income tax policies undoubtedly discourage reemployment. The return of even a portion of these women to active nursing would do much to lessen the effect of the shortage of nurses throughout this country. This is only one example of what could be achieved by permitting women to deduct the expenses of housekeeping and babysitting for income tax purposes. We are complaining because we lack sufficient numbers of medical personnel. Some people say we cannot launch the medicare plan because we do not have sufficient numbers of trained personnel. I can tell the minister that a great many nurses would be available right now if they were able to deduct for income tax purposes the expense of hiring a proper housekeeper. At present they cannot do so because of the expense which would be involved.
I should like the Minister of Finance to tell us why this should not be a legitimate busi-siness expense in the case of women working outside the home. Today 30 per cent of the labour force is made up of women. Why should they not have the same rights as men so far as deductions for income tax purposes on account of expenses are concerned? Certainly, a deduction in respect of housekeeping and babysitting expenses is one which might legitimately be claimed. The most effective way of enabling trained women to undertake important work is to allow them to deduct for income tax purposes the amounts paid in respect of housekeeping services.
I should like to hear whether the minister's ideas have changed in this regard. I would point out that more and more women are bringing pressure on us to recognize the case

June 12, 1967
Supply-Finance
for allowing expenses of this sort. Such a concession is only logical if these services are to be given without unnecessary anxiety as to the well-being of the families concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take this opportunity to make some comments on the general direction in which events in this country are moving. I do so on the basis of reports on Friday last showing a worsening in our balance of trade.
We have been saying for a long time that the government is permitting the cost of living to increase dramatically. I have the figures and I will produce them in a moment. Taxation in Canada has been increasing. The cost of government administration has been increasing in alarming fashion. The number of persons in the government service has increased dramatically-something like 12,000 within the past year. Government overhead expenses, the non-productive part of government, have been increasing faster than the productive portion of this country's economy.
All of us have been asking for months: Where is this leading and where will it end? I think we are beginning to see where it is leading. We have seen in the most recent return from the Dominion Bureau of Statistics evidence of a worsening of our trade position. During the months of April, 1966, imports amounted to $774 million. In the same months in 1967 imports amounted to $973 million, an increase of 25 per cent. It should also be said that there has been an increase in exports and for this, of course, we have to give credit where credit is due. But the increase in exports has not been sufficient to balance the increase in imports since a year ago when there was a small favourable balance amounting to slightly over $1 million. There is today an adverse balance amounting to over $73 million or, in terms of percentage, a 6,000 per cent increase. The result of the use of percentages gives an unreal figure but in fact that is what it amounts to. It is an indication that Canada is losing the fight to provide for its own people by means of its own productive capacity.
At the same time, employment is not increasing as it should and unemployment is increasing. It is not my purpose to stand here, as hon. members on the other side did for two or three years, beating away at the question of unemployment. They knew then, as they know now, that to a degree the unemployment figure is a false one. In many cases it does not mean hardship. Indeed, it is relatively meaningless in some respects because it is
[Mrs. Maclnnis (Vancouver-Kingsway) .1
calculated on the basis of the numbers looking for work. It is not related to destitution.
Nevertheless, we in Canada are increasing the cost of producing goods in this country to the point where we are not competitive with countries abroad. For some time we have been saying this would happen. Now it has happened, as the figures on external trade clearly show. If we were to take the figure for September last and compare it with a month earlier this year, the minister might say: There is a seasonal drop in April so you cannot compare the two months. But the hon. gentleman cannot say this drop is seasonal because I have been comparing identical months. It cannot be claimed that this is an odd or unusual situation because the import balance position has gradually been worsening as far as Canada is concerned. I am very worried in case we are gradually drifting toward the imperceptible point of no return at which we can import goods into Canada more cheaply than we can produce them. When that point comes, we buy more goods from countries abroad and sell less beyond our own borders.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I wonder whether the auto trade agreement has something to do with the situation. The minister may say it is temporary and that in the long run the auto trade agreement may work out to our benefit. But there are a lot of things the government has done about which it has said, "Well, in the long run, this is going to be better." We have to look at the figures which are given to us in this context.
According to the latest dominion bureau of statistics figures which were issued on Friday last, in 1966 we imported $72 million worth of motor vehicle parts. This year we have imported $98 million worth of parts, an increase of roughly $26 million. In 1966 we imported $24 million worth of what are referred to as new closed sedans. This year we have imported $63 million worth, an increase of roughly $40 million. Imports of trucks, tractors and chassis have risen this year to $8J million from $5i million in 1966. If this is the benefit we are getting from the auto trade pact, to me it does not seem to be much of a benefit. I could use other examples but I am not going to go into the details at this time.
These are not items for which the Minister of Finance is necessarily and primarily responsible. They are covered by government policy. But we are permitted to beat him over the head with them when discussing his estimates because it is his responsibility to see
June 12, 1967

that the budget is kept in accordance with the Canadian economy and to see that the economy of the country is kept viable through what the Department of Finance does. I never like being a prophet of doom. I hope the figures are all wrong. I hope we are making great progress, but I cannot see it in anything emanating from the dominion bureau of statistics.
Granted we sometimes take too much comfort or discomfort out of d.b.s. figures because from time to time they may not reflect the true picture. If we want to we can always make a case using d.b.s. figures, but the cost of living figures are very telling. In February, 1963, the year that the government took office, the cost of living index stood at 132.3. From 1957 until 1963 it increased by just over 11 points from 121.9 to 132.3. By 1964 it had increased to 134.5 and by February, 1967 it had risen to 146.1 an increase of 12 points within a few years. The figure for May of this year is 148.1, two full points above the February figure.
We know the reasons for the increase. It is partly due to free spending without real thought given to the productive value thereof. It is partly due to carelessness and neglect. We can blame programs and policies if we like, but with the government permitting the cost of living to increase so dramatically we are losing our ability to compete in world markets, and that ability is one of the fundamental bases of our economy. We are drifting, and I have seen no evidence from the minister's statements that the government is going to halt the drift and say, "Look, we are now at the critical point."
One of these days we are going to lose our markets. We are already starting to lose them. We are importing too many things. We have a great economy and we could maintain it by greater production. We rely on trade but there is something wrong with the current trend. It is going the wrong way and I take this opportunity to protest as strongly as I can. Our balance of trade figures are starting to show a bad trend. We are starting to lose the battle. When the saturation point is reached we will be in great difficulty.
I wish to conclude by referring to another subject. I have been very critical during the past year of the Industrial Development Bank for its lending policy, but in the last few months I have noticed that the officials are making a greater effort and I want to acknowledge that effort. I have noticed that more loans are being made to companies that
Canadian Wheat Board need help to become productive. I have noticed an increase in the amount of loans made to service the tourist industry, in which I am particularly interested. He said: Mr. Speaker, I introduce this motion somewhat reluctantly because the Canadian Wheat Board since 1935 when it came into being to handle Canadian grain because of very serious problems in respect of

June 12, 1967
Canadian Wheat Board price, has built up a very good reputation. At the time it came into being the farmers were not in a position to hold their wheat and sell when the price was high. Very often they had to sell at a lower price because of the need for money. At that time the Canadian Wheat Board handled only Canadian wheat but in 1949 oats and barley were also brought under the jurisdiction of the board.
This year I was a member of the delegation that flew to Russia on the inaugural flight of service between Canada and Russia by Aeroflot and Air Canada. We spent a few days in Russia, and as a result of being able to speak their language I found that many people there thought that the Canadian Wheat Board handled only wheat. They were not aware of the fact that in 1949 this board was given the authority to handle oats and barley as well as wheat.
There is a strong feeling in the three western prairie provinces that rapeseed and flaxseed should also be placed under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. It is my feeling that by changing the name to the Canada grain board we will indicate to people in foreign countries that this board handles not only wheat but all the other grains grown in this country. It may well be that this board will be given the authority before very long to handle other grains, and if the wrong impression which exists in foreign countries is allowed to continue we may lose many markets for these other grains. We now have markets in China, in Japan and in a number of European countries. I might say that Japan is our best customer for rapeseed.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, I brought forward this motion with some hesitation because of the fact that the Canadian Wheat Board has built up a good reputation and has helped the farmers of Canada save a great deal of money by finding markets for their products at stabilized prices. The time has come when the name should be changed. World demand for our grain is growing and if foreign countries have the impression that the Canadian Wheat Board handles only wheat we may lose a number of valuable customers.
I have discussed this matter with some members of the wheat board who feel a little bit reluctant about a name change because of its good reputation. Our customers know that if they buy a certain grade, whether it be No. 1, 2 or 3, through the Canadian Wheat Board they will receive that grade. On the other hand, if the name is not changed to make it

readily apparent to prospective customers that the board handles other grains as well our Canadian grain growers may lose these potential markets.
At the present time China and other countries buy mainly wheat from Canada but the time is coming when more rapeseed and other grains will be grown in Canada and markets will have to be found. For this reason I think all grains grown in the west should be brought under the same agency. I hope this motion will not be talked out and that consideration will be given to changing the name from the Canadian Wheat Board to the Canada grain board.

subtopic: PROPOSED RENAMING AS CANADA GRAIN BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a little time to discuss my hon. friend's notice of motion, and let me indicate at the outset that I am sure there is no desire on the part of any hon. member to do other than offer constructive criticism of the recommendation contained in this notice of motion. I want to confine my remarks to an analysis of the terms of the notice of motion and, for whatever help it may be, to indicate to hon. members the serious doubts I have as to whether it would be in the interest of the western Canadian producers of grain and the country generally to accept this motion at this time.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
I should like to direct my remarks to two aspects of the notice of motion. Perhaps I may do so, Mr. Speaker, by referring to its terms. I think the hon. member who is sponsoring the motion is trying to do two things. First, he states in his notice of motion:
That, in the opinion of this house-
I think this is the hon. member's first point.
-in order to remove any misunderstanding among foreign purchasers of Canadian grains to the effect that wheat only is handled by the Canadian Wheat Board-
I hope I am being fair to my hon. friend when I suggest this is the primary reason for the suggested change.
-the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation for the purpose of renaming the said board the "Canada Grain Board" and thereby indicate that other products such as oats, barley, flaxseed, rapeseed and rye are also handled by this board.
It would seem to me that the second objective of the notice of motion of my hon. friend is to bring about indirectly something that probably would not pass constitutional scrutiny if the house were to deal with it in this manner. Dealing with the argument of the
June 12, 1967

hon. member that the change of name should be made to make clear that the Canadian Wheat Board is not merely a wheat marketing agency, I think it would be wise to remind hon. members at this point that the Canadian Wheat Board is at this time a marketing agency in international and interprovincial trade in wheat, oats and barley.
I listened carefully to the argument of the sponsor of the notice of motion. I listened for evidence in support of the hon. member's argument. It was a good argument. However, I should like to have seen it supported by, for example, a resolution of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the National Farmers Union, or resolutions of other agricultural groups. I think this would have given the sponsor a much stronger argument to present to members of this house.
As I understood the argument of the hon. member it was based to a great extent on his own opinion. I respect the hon. member's opinion but would point out that it is the opinion of only one member of this house and it is unsupported by the sort of evidence that would have made it a much more compelling argument. It would have been a much more compelling argument if the hon. member could have backed it up with evidence such as I have indicated which might have been forthcoming from agricultural and producer groups.
I wish to make my first argument a positive one and say that I have great concern, and I think other members of this house have similar concern, about whether the change suggested in the notice of motion would create a great deal of confusion in the minds of the customers with whom the Canadian Wheat Board deals. I believe it would have this effect. My hon. friend who sponsored the notice of motion has indicated that such a change would be helpful in eliminating confusion but, with respect, Mr. Speaker, he did not give us any evidence to indicate that such confusion does in fact exist. I believe, therefore, that we would only be creating more confusion in making the change suggested.
I have a personal interest and a little knowledge in this matter because of some years spent in close association with the farming industry of Saskatchewan. I am very anxious to agree with my hon. friend about the reputation the Canadian Wheat Board has earned not only among the grain producers of western Canada but among the customers with whom the wheat board deals.
Canadian Wheat Board
I well recall, as does my hon. friend, the days before the Canadian Wheat Board was set up in western Canada. In those days there was in the marketing of wheat and other grains a great deal of confusion. It was not a form of marketing that was in the best interests of the producers. I join the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) and agree that the Canadian Wheat Board has done a good job in this respect. I suggest to hon. members that we would not want to detract from the good job the board has done. In particular we would not want to detract from the relationship of the Canadian Wheat Board with our international customers by changing the name of the board unless there was a good, concrete and compelling argument put forward for our so doing.
In this respect perhaps we should rely on the old saying that there is nothing that succeeds like success. I think hon. members will agree that the fact is that this is the record of the Canadian Wheat Board since its inception in 1935. In the marketing year 1965-66 the board visited 30 countries, some of them several times, in order to maintain the close contact it has with millers, grain traders and government officials in those markets. The hon. member did not suggest that there is confusion in the minds of the officials of approximately 100 countries of the world as to the functions of the board and what products it handles.
The second theme that I suggested is inherent in this notice of motion is one for which my hon. friend is well and properly noted and regarded in the house and throughout the country, at least throughout western Canada. I refer to the hon. member's record of championing the inclusion of other grains, particularly rapeseed, in the list of grains handled by the Canadian Wheat Board. I think the second objective of my friend is to introduce into the list of grains handled by the board flaxseed, rapeseed and rye because these are not not handled by the board in international and interprovincial trade. If we were to adopt the notice of motion it might be a basis for an argument that we were trying to accomplish in an indirect fashion something that the house has felt it advisable not to accomplish in a direct fashion when it has considered the matter. In my opinion the inclusion of flax, rye and rapeseed within the group of grains handled by the wheat board in international markets should be effected by an amendment to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. I think we should not try to make

June 12, 1967
Canadian Wheat Board changes of such magnitude through an indirect method.
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
As you know, Mr. Speaker, and as other hon. members know, the question of including other grains in the list that the Canadian Wheat Board is entitled to handle in export and interprovincial markets was considered by the house very recently during its examination of amendments to the Canadian Wheat Board Act. It would seem to me, and I make this suggestion to my friend, that if such a change were to be made it was at that time that it should have been made. In view of the fact it was not made at that time, it seems to me the house would not want to give any suggestion, indirect as it may be, of support for such a change at this time.
I do not make these suggestions in a negative sense, nor do I make them in a political sense. I think all members of the house recognize the sincerity with which the notice of motion has been advanced and the weight of argument, although I have been critical of it in some aspects, with which it has been put forth by the sponsor of the bill. However, I suggest that we should be very cautions in adopting this notice of motion. To do so might injure the great reputation which the Canadian Wheat Board has established for itself not only in Canada but throughout our trading markets in the international area.
Although I cannot document it at the present time, I think I am correct that the chairman of the Canadian Wheat Board, Mr. McNamara, when speaking before the agricultural and rural development committee, indicated a great lack of enthusiasm for any change. My recollection is that one of the arguments he used was that a change in name might have the effect of watering down the very substantial reputation which this agency has created for Canada in international markets.
I think there is no doubt that Canadians, particularly those in western Canada and those who have had relations with the Canadian Wheat Board, are of the opinion that this is probably the most successful and outstanding agency of the federal government that we have ever had in our history. I believe my hon. friend, the sponsor of the motion, would probably agree with that. In fact, he said the same thing in different words. In no way would I want my remarks to be interpreted as being critical of the Canadian Wheat Board. All I wish to say is that I think

the house should zealously guard the reputation which the board has established for itself both in Canada and abroad.
The last matter I want to mention briefly is one to which I referred earlier. My hon. friend's argument would have been much more substantial had he been able to produce definite evidence of a desire for such a change on the part of the people directly concerned with the operations of the wheat board. To my knowledge the producer groups and the agricultural agencies of western Canada who are most directly concerned with the operations of the board have not indicated any such desire. It seems to me, and I hope hon. members will concur, that until the sponsor, other hon. members or, indeed, the government receive representations from these interested groups that it would be in the interest of the western producers and of Canada generally to make such a change, it is not one of the functions of the house to change the name of an agency which has established a sound reputation for well over 30 years, is acknowledged throughout the world and is particularly appreciated by the producers whom it serves.

Mr. Speaker, I was particularly interested in the remarks of the last speaker who seemed to indicate that if the house took some action on this motion it would immediately produce some result. I point out that the key words in the motion are, "the government should consider the advisability of introducing legislation". I do not see how anyone can object to the consideration of the advisability of introducing legislation. I am of the opinion that the house should be willing to consider almost anything and there should be no fear of considering the matter.
The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) mentioned that he had introduced several times the proposal to consider the addition of rapeseed and other grains to the grains handled by the Canadian Wheat Board. If it were not for the fact that I have been here a long time and heard the predecessor of the hon. member for Hum-boldt-Melfort-Tisdale refer on numerous occasions to rapeseed in a very decided and knowledgeable way, I might be prepared one of these days to introduce a motion to change the name of rapeseed to "rappseed".
Two points should be taken into consideration in examining the proposed change of name from Canadian Wheat Board to Canada
June 12, 1967

grain board. First there is the sentimental aspect attached to the name of the wheat board. As the previous speaker has indicated, many farmers in western Canada would be opposed to changing the name to Canada grain board on the basis of the fact that this is one of the few government agencies about which more favourable than critical comments are made. I think that in the main most farmers, most politicians and in fact the majority of the Canadian people accept the Canadian Wheat Board as a viable and very useful implement of the government. For this reason a sentimental and historical attachment surrounds the name of the Canadian Wheat Board. This is the opinion of the president of the Canadian Wheat Board who, as the previous speaker mentioned, has shown little enthusiasm for a change in the name of the board. Incidentally, I find he shows little enthusiasm for any change. For that reason I discount his objection to this change.
The reason this matter should be referred to the committee and why the government should give it consideration is that I believe we could probably solve the problem much better by changing the name of the board to the "Canadian wheat and grain board". Even this does not go far enough because of the simple fact that at present oats and barley are included under the act and these are cereal grains. However, this name would not include other grains such as flax, rapeseed and grass seed which, we normally call grains and which are mechanically handled in the same way as other grains but which are not in the same botanical category.
[DOT] (6:30 p.m.)
We in the agricultural field consider these grains and seeds to be in the all embracing category of grain. However, there are those who say that grains should be the botanical grains, and the others should be considered as seeds of the oil bearing type. It may therefore be necessary to add grains and oil seeds to the title of the board, so we might get a very complicated name that would not only confuse the farmers but would confuse the board and everybody else. For this reason I agree that there has to be some consideration given to changing the name. It would seem to me that the name might be changed to the Canadian grain board. However, such a change would not accomplish the purpose of the hon. member who introduced this motion.

However, I agree with the hon. member that this is a subject which could well be given to the committee for study to ascertain the effect of such a change upon our domestic population and our customers abroad. If, as the hon. member states, the customers who are interested in purchasing these other grains from us are of the opinion they could not do this with the wheat board, then I feel the wheat board has been negligent in issuing propaganda throughout the world. This board has the responsibility of handling oats and barley. I was of the opinion they were marketing as much of these products as they could. If the suggestion is to change the name to assist in extending the sales of these products, then I feel this measure would be worthy of committee study.

June 12, 1967
Canadian Wheat Board
I, Mr. Speaker, would be opposed to accepting this motion as an amendment at the present time, but I believe it could well receive the support of the house if the subject matter were referred to a committee for further study. It is becoming more and more important, with increasing production, that coarse grains and oil seeds should be handled by a board. speechtext:
My remarks will be very brief with regard to this motion, which has been presented by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp). I am somewhat amazed at the arguments that have been presented, particularly some of those presented by the hon. member for Durham (Mr. Honey) and some of those presented by the hon. member for Timis-kaming (Mr. Peters), although I agree with the latter speaker's basic analysis of the situation. I think I have some familiarity with the agricultural situation in the west. All the farmer in the west is asking is that other grains, including rye, rapeseed and flaxseed, be given the same marketing and handling facilities as the wheat board has provided for wheat. This is not a criticism in any way of the wheat board, but I think it is an expression of the value of some of the facilities it has provided to the wheat grower in western Canada.
I can well understand the hon. member seeking to have this subject referred to the agriculture committee. I hope, too, the agriculture committee of the Liberal caucus will consider it, because it seems to me it is a very practical suggestion. It is not one, really, in which sentiment is involved, although I can understand how sentiment might be involved on the part of those farmers who have been more or less satisfied with what the wheat board has done.
We want the name of the board to represent the actual functions the board is expected to carry out. If other grains have been added to the responsibility of the wheat board, if it is logical to assume the same service is going to be extended to include flaxseed, rapeseed and rye, then it is only reasonable that the name be changed to reflect the two functions of the board. Surely in the years ahead the wheat board is going to be concerned not only with marketing wheat but also these other grains and seeds.

[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
It seems to me that the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale should be commended for bringing the motion before us at this time. I hope the house can accept it because all he is requesting is that the government give consideration to changing the name of the wheat board to a more distinctive title. Now that the wheat board has taken on a more permanent structure-and it is good this is so-I think it is all the more urgent that consideration be given to this question. The hon. member for Timiskaming has already mentioned that the agriculture committee had this question brought before it at various points during its trip to the west, and it is certainly one that should be given further consideration by the committee and by parliament. The very fact that it has been brought up is indicative that there is genuine worth in the motion before the house now, and I hope hon. members will accept it.

subtopic: PROPOSED RENAMING AS CANADA GRAIN BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since we are considering today motion No. 5, the purpose of which is to rename the Canadian Wheat Board, I wish to make known my views fully.
I first want to congratulate the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) who is certainly an expert in the field of western agriculture in general, and especially, with regard to the growing of rapeseed. Besides, he is the proposer of that motion.
I was able to appreciate his knowledge during a trip to the western provinces with other hon. members, members of the committee on agriculture, forestry and rural development.
During our meetings, he explained to us on many occasions the significance of rapeseed.
However, before voting on such a piece of legislation, I think that we ought to give it further consideration.

There are several other points that should be brought up in a discussion such as that brought on by the motion that now occupies our deliberations. We should consider the implications of the fact that the bulk of our coarse grains production is actually consumed within Canada, whereas the bulk of our wheat production is exported overseas. The Canadian Wheat Board's agents are, of course, members of the grain trade whose Canadian headquarters are to a great extent located in Winnipeg, close to that board. The
June 12, 1967

bulk of the sales of Canadian grain are made by these grain firms acting as export agents for the Canadian Wheat Board.
Of course when the state trading nations are in the market they do approach the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Canadian Wheat Board in the first instance in order to arrive at an over-all agreement. But by and large the Canadian Wheat Board rely on their agents to sell the bulk of the wheat exports. In like manner I suppose they look to these same companies to merchandize oats and barley.
It therefore seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that while I would take nothing away from the Canadian Wheat Board as far as their excellent reputation in world grain circles is concerned, I would nevertheless have to believe that an equally fine reputation is needed by each and every one of the export grain firms who act as the export selling agents for the board. Those reputations, coupled to that of Canadian grain, are responsible in large measure for the successful marketing operations carried out on behalf of Canadian grain producers.
That would appear to bring me to the second theme that I detected in the motion now before us, namely the handling of flax, rye and rapeseed by the Canadian Wheat Board. During the recent debate on Bill No. C-106, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, several members brought un the subject of putting flax, rye and rapeseed under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board, making that board the sole marketing agency for those grains. I was somewhat surprised. Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Hum-boldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) did not rise on that occasion to bring to the attention of hon. members once again his ideas concerning either the changing of the name of the board or the matter of giving the board jurisdiction over flaxseed, rye and rapeseed.
The hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Jorgenson) was one of those who took the trouble to bring to the attention of the members of this house the inclusion of flax, rye and rapeseed under the provisions of the Canadian Wheat Board Act. He correctly explained that a problem does exist, in that the board applies delivery quota restrictions to the deliveries of rye and flaxseed in particular. He mentioned that a recommendation had been submitted in the report of the standing committee on agriculture, forestry and rural development at the close of the last session.
Canadian Wheat Board
My reading of the committee's report, Mr. Speaker, leads me to believe that what the committee was actually recommending was not that these other grains should be brought under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board, but that at least a plebiscite should be held, probably in like manner to those held several years ago in Australia. And again of course some enabling legislation from provincial governments would be required before any action could be taken. This is very important, and I feel that all members should bear in mind the constitutional problems inherent in these marketing shemes.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, I am not among those who would be in any haste to change the name of the Canadian Wheat Board. I do not stand with those who would impose upon the grain producers of western Canada the obligation to deliver all their marketings of all their grains to the board; nor, indeed, would I be in any haste to require of the board that they be the sole buyer of these farm products. I do not believe sufficient study has yet been given to either of these matters. We realize that we really do not have an idea of what is likely to be the impact of a change in the board's name. Nor are we yet well enough acquainted with the possibility of improvements to net farm income if the Canadian Wheat Board were to become the sole buyer and initial seller of virtually all grain grown in western Canada.
One further point that should be made, Mr. Speaker, is the confusion that the change in name of the board could generate in the minds of overseas customers, between the Canada grain board-the name suggested by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale-and the Board of Grain Commissioners for Canada. The similarity between the two names is already confusing enough, even to members of this house, many of whom do not have a clear idea of the jurisdiction and responsibilities of each of these boards. The change in name would not improve this situation but would I suggest only aggravate it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion introduced by the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale (Mr. Rapp) seems to deal with at least two points. The first concerns the changing of the name of the Canadian Wheat Board. The second point is more subtle and concerns the different grains which would be handled by this board.

June 12, 1967
Canadian Wheat Board
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian Wheat Board Act, or Bill No. C-106, which gave rise to several debates in this house recently, mentions wheat, oats and barley only, whereas the motion now before us deals with the sale of wheat, oats, barley, flaxseed, rapeseed and rye which the Canadian Wheat Board might handle for the western producers.
When the directors of the Canadian Wheat Board testified before the standing committee on agriculture, forestry and rural development, in February last, in the city of Winnipeg, the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale asked the chairman of the Canadian Wheat Board, Mr. McNamara, what were his views concerning a new name for the board. Here is what Mr. McNamara answered him, and I quote:
[DOT] (6:50 p.m.)

All I can say is that a rose by any other name would smell as sweet and I hope we would smell just as sweet in the eyes of the world as we do now in being called the Canadian Wheat Board. I assume this developed from the pool organizations calling themselves wheat pools, but handling all grains. The Australian wheat board merchandizes only wheat. There is an Australian barley board which is a separate organization. But I am surprised to hear you say that in your visit abroad you ran into people who do not realize we are also interested in marketing Canadian barley and oats and that we are also interested in doing what v/e can to market flax, rapeseed and develop business generally for Canada in these markets. As I say, I never thought about changing our name. In a commercial organization, if you have a product that is well known in the world, whether it is White Rose flour or something like that, you try to capitalize on your reputation. I am just vain enough to think that the reputation of the Canadian Wheat Board throughout the world is such that we should continue to capitalize on it.
And there you have, Mr. Speaker, the opinion of the chief commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board, which he has led so ably and so successfully during the last ten years or so, on the matter of changing the name of the Canadian Wheat Board to the Canada grain board.

I wonder, Mr. Speaker, what the western farmers would think if the name of the board were changed, since this name is known all over the world.

It is interesting to note that the Australian experience has been somewhat like our own. In 1935, which happens to be the year that the present Canadian Wheat Board was

inaugurated, the Commonwealth of Australia tried to set up a wheat marketing board having trading powers, and legislation was actually passed by the commonwealth parliament. However the privy council made the plan unworkable in a decision that declared that section 92 of the Australian constitution bound the commonwealth equally with the states. I am sure hon. members will find no difficulty in seeing the parallel here.
Upon the outbreak of war in 1939, the commonwealth government established the Australian wheat board, giving it complete trading powers. So it is evident that while the Australian wheat board was first established under national security regulations at the beginning of the second world war, it could not have continued in existence without some further action to get them over their constitutional obstacle. In Australia plebiscites have been held twice since the war on the question of the introduction of a wheat stablization plan involving the retention of the Australian wheat board as the sole marketing authority. These ballots indicated that the Australian wheat growers were in favour of the plan. Since the last ballot in 1953, grower's support has been so evident that ballots have not been considered necessary.
I bring this to the attention of hon. members, Mr. Speaker, to indicate that we are not the only nation with constitutional problems concerning the marketing of our agricultural products. I really did not intend to go further in this description of the Australian experience, Mr. Speaker, but I find it so very fascinatingly close to our own experience that I would ask your indulgence for a few moments more to add just one or two further sentences about the Australian situation.
The Australian wheat board, like our own, has a monopoly trading powers. The growers are required to deliver to it all wheat other than that retained for seed or feed on the farm where it is produced. The wheat board negotiates export sales direct with overseas buyers. However sales to the United Kingdom, Europe, the Middle East and India are usually made through the Australian wheat committee, an agency of the Australian wheat board located in London. Wheat flour is sold overseas by private traders under the general control of the Australian wheat board. Where their board differs from the Canadian Wheat Board is in the matter of the grains they handle. In Australia, the wheat board is concerned only with wheat. As hon. members are quite aware, the Canadian wheat board is the sole initial buyers of western wheat, oats and
June 12, 1967

barley that enter commercial channels crossing interprovincial and international boundaries.
There is an Australian barley board, Mr. Speaker, but its name is a legacy from the second world war. In Canada, the Canadian Wheat Board was originally established to handle only wheat. In the beginning this was on a voluntary basis, and did not become compulsory until September, 1943, when the Canadian Wheat Board became the sole marketing agency for wheat produced in the designated area. It was not until August 1, 1949, that the Canadian Wheat Board became the sole marketing agency for oats and barley produced and sold in the prairie provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta.

Mr. Chairman, I did not make an opening statement because it is only a few days since I presented the budget, and I felt that it would promote better and more thorough consideration of the estimates if I were to reply to questions rather than to make another speech on the subjects on which I wished to give a dissertation. I am grateful, however, to the committee for calling the finance estimates somewhat earlier than usual. It is customary in our proceedings for the finance estimates to go through at the last minute when no one has any time left, and the minister of finance is not given an opportunity of answering some of the questions that ought to be answered and of defending more adequately the policies that he administers. Therefore I propose, Mr. Chairman, to deal with some of the questions that have been raised tonight.
Perhaps, however, I ought to make one general comment at the beginning, and that is that I do not look upon this as an extension of the budget debate, and if I do not deal with some of the questions relating to technical matters of taxation it is because I think it would be better for me to do this in an orderly fashion when the budget is under discussion.

That is right, but I have to defend that decision in the budget debate and will deal with those questions then.
The hon. member for Edmonton West began his remarks by referring to monetary developments, and he asked me in effect if I would make some projections of interest rates. This of course I would not do since, like other people in the financial world, I do not know what will happen to interest rates. However, I would like to make one or two comments in reply to some of the specific points he made.
Since the passage of the Bank Act, and even during its passage, interest rates began to decline and there was quite a marked drop both in short and long term rates. As I recall it, the rates on treasury bills, for example, declined from levels well in excess of 5 per cent down to less than 4 per cent. Subsequently they have increased again moderately and are now in the neighbourhood of 4.4 per cent, or something of that kind.
June 12, 1967

Interest rates on long term also declined quite significantly, but not to the same extent, nor did we expect that they would, even in a period of easier monetary conditions and declining interest rates. They have in fact gone up again, not to the high levels that were attained last year, but they have responded in the main to influence in the United States, where long term interest rates are about at the level that they attained at the height of the monetary squeeze. It is of course impossible for Canadian interest rates to diverge very widely from the United States because we are, and will continue, so far as I can see into the future, to be a capital importing country. Therefore we must have a scale of interest rates in relation to the United States that enables us to borrow in that country to meet our requirements.
The hon. member also asked about the interest ceiling under the Bank Act. As he will recall, section 91 of the Bank Act as approved at the last session, provided that the interest rate ceiling would be removed when average of the market yield on short term bonds of Canada for all Wednesdays in any period of three months ending after December 31, 1966, was less than 5 per cent. In fact the average of the market yield on short term bonds of Canada did fall below an average of 5 per cent during a period of three months and therefore, in the parlance of the street, the trigger has released, and it has been announced publicly that after December 31, 1967, there will be no ceiling on bank interest rates.
As hon. members know, during the time since the passage of the Bank Act there has been a very great increase in competition among the banks, and between the banks and other financial institutions. Indeed the complaints that I have heard, perhaps more than others have heard, are complaints about the competition, particularly from other institutions that are finding they are no longer protected as they were by the Bank Act and now have to compete for their funds with the banks.
The banks have increased the interest they are paying on deposits, and immediately after the Bank Act came into effect they reduced the prime rate from the prevailing rate of 6 per cent down to 5f per cent. As expected, and as was intended, interest rates charged by the banks are no longer uniform. They differ between institutions and they differ in accordance with the credit rating of the borrower so that you have a range of interest rates going from a prime rate of 5| per
Supply-Finance
cent up to the present ceiling of 1\ per cent.
Moreover the banks have been moving in a massive way into housing loans from which previously they were excluded. Therefore the Bank Act is having, as we intended, a very marked effect upon bank practices, upon the service the banks are able to perform for the public, and most of all there has been an enormous increase in the competition among them and between them and other institutions, this for the benefit of the public, e (8:20 p.m.)
The hon. member also asked if I would refer the regulations under the deposit insurance act to the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. I apologize for not having done so earlier. It is my intention to do so, and I shall forthwith. The reason I did not do this earlier is because the committee was not organized, and when I spoke to the chairman he asked me not to do so until the committee was under way. It is now under way and I will be happy to refer these regulations and whatever other matters it might be useful to have the committee discuss. It is my opinion that it would be very useful for the public's education to have these regulations under the deposit insurance act scrutinized, and I believe it would also be useful for the education of the public to look at other regulations in respect of consumer loans. All of these matters deserve public airing, and that can only do good.
As I understood the hon. member for Edmonton West, he said he hoped the legislation to establish the Canada Development Corporation would be lost in the shuffle. I regret to disappoint him, because that is not my intention. It is my intention to proceed with the Canada Development Corporation legislation as soon as we can find a place for it on the order paper.

I can assure hon. members that the legislation is almost ready to present and it will be presented shortly after we resume. Those are not all the comments I wish to make in reply to the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton West, but I will reserve some of my other comments in order that I can deal with his remarks together with those made by other members on the same subject.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowi-chan-The Islands made some comments about the Bank Act, in respect of which he as well

June 12, 1967
Supply-Finance
as other members ol the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, are now somewhat expert. That committee did an extremely good job of work on the Bank Act and there are now many members of this house who know a great deal more than they originally did about the workings of our banking system and the effect of the Bank Act upon those institutions and others with which they compete.
I do hope that hon. gentlemen will agree that there has been a very big change in the way in which the banks have operated since the passage of the Bank Act amendments. I will not say that competition has been restored, because it never existed, but it has been established. I expect in the next few years to see changes in our whole financial structure arising out of this new kind of competition, changes that even now we cannot foresee or envisage.
The hon. member made some comment about splitting of shares. I inquired during the dinner interval as to whether either the inspector general of banks or I had any responsibility, or whether we had to give any approval, and I found that neither of us has any responsibility in this regard under the Bank Act. While I recognize there are many reasons for splitting the shares, I do think it is important that in respect of institutions like banks the price of the shares should not be so high as to discourage investment by relatively small investors. Therefore, I believe that splitting of shares, while this may be in the interest of existing shareholders, is also in the interest of maintaining as wide a distribution of these shares as possible.
The hon. member also referred to near banks. I hope he has followed very closely the developments which have taken place in connection with the application of deposit insurance, because I do suggest to him and to other members of the committee, particularly those who took such a close interest in this matter while the legislation was under discussion, that developments have been pretty much as predicted.
Federal deposit insurance is now in effect in respect of all publicly incorporated companies and all provincially incorporated companies, except those incorporated in the province of Quebec, under arrangements made between the other provinces and Ottawa, so that deposit insurance in so far as nine of the ten provinces are concerned is operating just as we hoped it would. There was a short time when, because of the pressure of events, and
TMr. Sharp.]
because of some undesirable developments in the financial world in respect of certain Ontario companies, Ontario deposit insurance came into effect as an interim measure. However as the Ontario government minister said, as soon as the federal legislation was available the insurance was transferred from Ontario to the federal institution.
Let me suggest to the hon. member for Edmonton West as well as the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands that the attitude of Quebec toward deposit insurance does support the argument that I made both in the house and before the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, that if we had introduced legislation to bring near banks under federal jurisdiction, using the power that we believe Ottawa has in connection with banking, that legislation would have been challenged and today there would not have been the degree of supervision over deposit taking institutions which exists in nine of the ten provinces.
That was one of the reasons the government decided deposit insurance was the most practical step to take. At least this brought the institutions in nine of the ten provinces under supervision and gave the depositors there a greater assurance of safety in respect of their deposits than they had before. If we had proceeded to legislate in respect of near banks, that legislation would certainly have been challenged by Quebec, which even now challenges our jurisdiction in respect of deposit insurance and thus held up the whole legislation. By following the procedure we did, by which institutions could only come under federal insurance with the approval of the provinces, we have avoided the kind of stalemate I do not think any one would want to have seen.
Perhaps I could go on to the next point made by the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, about the Mercantile Bank. The committee will recall that at the last minute in our discussions of the Bank Act amendments a proposal was made that the extension of time should be subject to review by the governor in council. We have not yet had an application from the Mercantile Bank for an extension of time beyond December 31, 1967. I have indicated to such of the directors as have happened to see me that this approval would not be given unless the Mercantile Bank put before us its plans for the disposal of stock. In other words, I have made it quite clear, as I said in the house and before the Senate committee when the bill
June 12, 1967

was before the other place, that the extension of time was given for a particular purpose. I quite agree with what the member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands said, that the most regrettable thing that could happen would be for the Mercantile Bank to proceed to expand, and for us to find at the end of a period of five years that nothing had happened, and no effort had been made to dispose of the shares, in order that they could get out from under the restrictions, or find an extended basis on which to support their deposits. I believe that parliament acted very wisely in restricting that approval to the prior approval of the governor in council from time to time.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Perhaps I may return to a point made by the hon. member for Edmonton West and the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, namely the state of play in the discussions of international liquidity. I believe the members of the committee are well enough aware of the history of these consultations that I need not take the time now to go through all that history except to remind the committee that deputies of the ministers and governors of the Group of Ten-which vire the ten most important countries, from the financial point of view, in the world -were instructed in October, 1963, to undertake a thorough examination of the outlook for the functioning of the international monetary system and of its probable future needs for liquidity. That is the instruction upon which the Group of Ten ministers and their deputies have been operating. There have been various developments. I have had the privilege of sitting in on one or two of the meetings since I have been minister, and I have in front of me an official who was at all the meetings.
Last September, at the meeting of the governors of the International Monetary Fund, it was proposed that the executive board of the International Monetary Fund should meet with the deputies to attend a meeting of the Group of Ten. These meetings have been held. There have been three joint sessions of two or three days each and another is scheduled to take place in Paris next week. I expect I will be asked, as minister, to attend the meeting of the Group of Ten in July. Efforts have been made to find a suitable date and I am not quite sure which day in July it will be, but it looks as if something will be possible about the middle of that month. Then, of course, we will be reporting again at
Supply-Finance
the International Monetary Fund meetings in Rio in September.
I think it is fair to say that most of the technical studies necessary to establish a new reserve asset have now been made. What is needed now is agreement amongst governments as to the major characteristic of the new asset. The basic point at issue is what, if any, condition should be attached to the new asset affecting its use and transfer ability. Speaking as the Canadian minister, as one of the Group of Ten, I am inclined to a more unconditional kind of transfer ability. I would hope that at a meeting of the ministers and the governors that I have been speaking about, and at the annual meeting in Rio of the governors of the International Monetary Fund, further progress will be made in resolving differences amongst governments on these matters.
I should like to make one point clear because of a remark that was made during these discussions. The new asset would not replace any of the existing forms of reserves. It certainly would not replace gold, and it would not replace the United States dollar; and in so far as sterling is used as a reserve currency, it would not replace sterling. It would be an addition to the assets that are available to finance world trade and world payments.
The hon. member for Simcoe East put forward a very strong appeal for further support for the teaching of doctors, and generally for the support of the training of medical personnel. I could not help remarking, as I listened to the hon. member, that this is an example of what I said in my budget speech, of worthy but expensive projects that add to government spending and is one of the reasons why there is a problem not only in Ottawa but in all the provincial capitals and in all city councils, namely of trying to find enough money to do all the good things we would like to do.
Personally I agree with the hon. member. I would like to see more resources devoted to this purpose. I have been moderately encouraging to some of the doctors who have come to me in search of support of medical research, which is another aspect of the same problem. May I add that this is the first time it has been said in this house that I insisted upon medicare coming into effect on July 1, 1968. Most of the criticisms I have heard have been to the opposite effect, that I insisted upon its postponement until July 1, 1968. I am very, very grateful to the hon. member for having put this problem into perspective.

June 12. 1987

It is always delightful to hear the hon. member for Kootenay West. I hope his party enjoyed his speech of this afternoon as much as I did. He made one or two comments about credit unions and asked whether there should not be a national credit unions act. I would point out to him that in fact there is one. At the federal level there is the Co-operative Credit Associations Act which provides for the incorporation by special act of the parliament of Canada of co-operative credit societies. I might add that amendments to this act are under consideration at the present time. This is one of the reasons why, when we brought forward the deposit insurance legislation, I did not include credit unions as the sort of deposit-taking institutions that would be subject to insurance. It seemed to me that they were of a different character, and what we think would be more appropriate for the development and assistance in the development of those institutions would be

facilities by which they might be able to obtain loans to increase their liquidity when they needed it. After all, these are not deposit-taking institutions in the ordinary sense. They deal with their own members, and you have to become a member of the co-operative before you can have deposits with it.
* (8:40 p.m.)
I have answered a great many questions in the house on the subject of perpetual bonds and I do not think there is very much that I can add. Like other hon. members, I have received many letters. Indeed, for a while, they formed a very high proportion of my correspondence. It would appear there were many people who purchased these bonds originally, or perhaps even at later stages, who misunderstood their character. They were intended to be perpetual bonds. When they were issued they were considered to be excellent buys, indeed they went to a premium. It is difficult for us to realize now that when these bonds were issued some 30 odd years ago a 3 per cent rate of interest forever looked like a wonderful bargain when the short term rate of interest was 1 per cent. However, they were intended to be perpetual bonds. The government looked at the possibility of paying them off on a selective basis, but after thoroughly examining each one of these alternatives we came to the conclusion that the only way we could deal fairly with all concerned was to treat them as what they are, namely perpetual bonds that never have to be paid off. They vary in price in accordance with the interest rates on the market. When you can get 4, 5 or 6 per cent on other forms of investment, of course you will not buy these perpetual bonds which yield 3 per cent for more than 50, 60 or 70 per cent of their value. But if interest rates were to go down again to levels around the 3 per cent, which is conceivable, as interest rates are essentially unpredictable, then these bonds would again rise in value to somewhere near par. We thought of paying off those individuals who bought the bonds originally and held them until now, but that would be unfair to those who had been advised to sell them earlier. They would have as great a claim upon the government as those who held them. So in the end we had to decide that even though we knew there were people who had been misled in buying these bonds, in order to deal fairly and in the interests of all concerned we had to treat them as perpetuals, which is what they are.
June 12, 1967

I thank you, Mr. Chairman and members of the committee. I will pass over the comments of the Leader of the Opposition and come back to them later.
I should now like to deal with some of the specific points raised by the hon. member for Parkdale. He suggested that there might be some exemption for the interest on certain types of bonds issued by municipalities. We have examined that proposition from time to time and have come to the conclusion that it amounts to an indirect subsidy to the municipalities. It seemed to us that if we were going to give subsidies to municipalities, it should be done on a much more logical basis and in accordance with a government policy, and not just because a municipality decided it was going to issue some bonds now, whereas another municipality which had issued its bonds earlier would not have the advantage of a tax free status.
On the question of whether there should be a deduction on home owners' taxable income, we have looked at the matter from time to time and found that it has one obvious fault, namely that it is a suggestion which favours one particular kind of resident, that is one who happens to own his home and not rent it. Of course this is not fair, particularly to those who live in apartment buildings. So I felt that as Minister of Finance I could not recommend to the government the proposals put before me by the mayor of Toronto, which have been mentioned by the hon. member for Parkdale.
The hon. member for Parkdale asked me for a report on the claims of Canadian citizens on foreign governments for the settlement of nationalization claims and other matters of that kind. Perhaps I could give a brief progress report. We have completed our negotiations with Bulgaria. A settlement was made last year and announced in June, 1966. Negotiations are now in progress with Hungary. Indeed a Hungarian delegation is in Ottawa now. Czechoslovakia and Rumania have now both agreed to enter into negotiations. Canadian claimants have been asked to submit the details of their claims. With Poland, with whom the negotiations have been
Supply-Finance
perhaps more difficult than with any other country, these negotiations, which have been under way for some time, are to be resumed after a break. We now believe that they can be resumed within the next few weeks or months.
As I said, I will not deal with questions of taxation policy. I think these should be dealt with in the budget debate.
The hon. member for Vancouver East raised a general question about government bonds and the investments of individuals who find, when they want to realize these bonds, that they have declined in price. This related not only to perpetual bonds but to all market issues of Canadian bonds. All I can say to the committee is that this is why Canada savings bonds were created. Today very few people of modest circumstances buy market issues of Canadian government bonds because of the fluctuations which take place in their price. Now they buy Canada savings bonds which can be cashed at their face value at any time.
The hon. member for Perth asked me how we were going to finance ourselves in the next year. He will realize that it is not possible to predict in advance the exact amount of any particular bond issue, even a bond issue which is only a refunding issue. However, I can say that in general I do expect to refund all maturities coming due during this fiscal year. In the white paper which appeared with the budget there is a list of the unmatured debt, from which one can get a list of all the bonds that are maturing this year. These maturities, coming due during the remainder of this fiscal year, will total $525 million on October 1, 1967, and $515 million on January 15, 1968. As to the new issues for cash which the hon. member understands I will have to make, I cannot add anything to what I have said in my budget address.
He also asked about church vestments and inquired about the item which appears among the resolutions in the budget. I am answering this question because I understand there is an inquiry about its meaning, but I will not discuss the policy. In fact, the rate on church vestments was reduced to 10 per cent in 1960. All that this resolution does is to bring parts of vestments into line at the same rate. So there should be no reason why the customs officials should not just proceed to enter church vestments at the prevailing rate of 10 per cent.
The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka drew attention to the April figures on imports. I should like to point out to him,

speechtext: I deny this; there has never been such a generous arrangement of financial affairs between the federal government and the provinces. This results from a much greater generosity in connection with these claims, as well as the fact that this arrangement which is in effect now is neutral. It does not select any one tax, it selects the whole range of provincial taxes and equals them up to the provincial average. In the course of this development Saskatchewan has been moving toward being one of the "have" provinces and is not any longer entitled to payments from Ottawa. For that reason, we have arranged a system of graduated payments so as to phase Saskatchewan out of the very large payments she has been getting. Supply-Finance
Municipal Grants Act.
