maintopic: CONSUMER CREDIT-INQUIRY AS TO LEGISLATION THIS SESSION
CONSUMER CREDIT-INQUIRY AS TO LEGISLATION THIS SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 1 I asked the Registrar General whether he intended to introduce legislation in this session to incorporate any of the recommendations of the joint committee on consumer credit. To say the least, the reply of the minister was pretty vague. Certainly he gave no indication that action would be taken this session. This is a matter which is of great concern to many people. Members of parliament have been increasingly aware of the tremendous problems faced by people, particularly those in the low income groups. The result was that over the years as many as a dozen bills were introduced by various members of the house, from all parties, which had the object of controlling the rate of interest, calling for the publication of the true rate of interest, and controlling the door to door sale of merchandise so as to give people the opportunity to cancel the contract, if they signed one, to purchase things without real, knowledge of the facts.
So insistent were the complaints, Mr. Speaker, that the government finally agreed to the establishment of a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate to study the question of consumer credit. This committee was chaired jointly by Senator Croll and the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Greene), the hon. member for Renfrew South. The committee held its first meeting on June 2, 1964, more than three years ago. So important was the subject which the committee was considering that the committee recommended, and the house approved for the first time, the hiring of expert staff. The committee had working with it a chartered accountant and a lawyer who were able to give the committee expert advice.
The committee heard representations from a large number of organizations representing the retail trade, the finance companies, credit unions, co-operatives, government agencies such as the superintendent of insurance and the Bank of Canada, consumers associations, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and a host of others. It became obvious that it was necessary for the government to move into this field by passing legislation.


The committee was confronted by evidence that people were paying 20 per cent to 30 per cent interest; that people were borrowing money or purchasing goods when they did not have the slightest idea of the amount of interest they were paying; that people were purchasing goods and the companies selling the goods were selling the contracts for the collection of money to a third agency; that sometimes the merchandise was inferior and even after it was returned the people were still required to pay the money they had contracted to pay. The committee made a series of recommendations concerning the type of legislation that should be passed.
Before I go to that, I want to point out that the committee found what many lawyers already knew, namely that the field of jurisdiction was divided between the federal and provincial governments. The provinces have begun to move in this field. In the Finanaal Post of April 15, 1965 a story appeared which summarized the legislation being considered or already passed by the provinces of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. These provinces have either passed or are considering the passage of legislation covering their jurisdiction.
Now, the committee made some excellent recommendations. It recommended for example that legislation be passed which would spell out what had been commonly referred to as truth in lending so people would know exactly the total cost of credit expressed both in a lump sum and in terms of simple annual interest. The committee recommended that the advertisements which offered credit should be required to set out annual percentage rates, as well as in dollars and cents, the cost to the consumer for the use of money. The committee recommended also that the protection accorded to borrowers under the small loans act be increased from the present limit of $1,500 up to $5,000. Incidentally this recommendation was made by the Porter commission.
The committee recommended a cooling off period of three days for reconsideration by the purchaser of goods on credit from other sources than stores. This committee recommended terms upon which a purchaser may, without penalty, return goods or recover any moneys paid by him, and so on. This was an excellent report.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
We now have a department of consumer affairs which will be in the charge of the
June 12, 1967

Registrar General. To my knowledge, Mr. Speaker, no minister has had the kind of publicity that the Registrar General has had. Every newspaper and magazine in Canada has been filled with stories about the great things the Registrar General is going to do. The Financial Post for April 15 carried a story which summarized the ideas the minister had about amending the combines act to give it new and sharper key, extending the legislation to cover service industries and to open the way for injured parties in price fixing cases to sue in civil courts for damages. Then the minister promised a complete review of the Canada Corporation Act, and so on.
Here is a committee which has gone in great detail into a very important field affecting most of the people in Canada, particularly those in the lower income groups.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION-U.S. CITIZENS IN CANADA TO ESCAPE ARMY DRAFT
IMMIGRATION-U.S. CITIZENS IN CANADA TO ESCAPE ARMY DRAFT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker. I have a question to bring before the house which is considered the highest court in the land. Before I give some details you might be interested in knowing that the department of immigration has known for some days that I was to raise a question tonight regarding a Greek citizen now visiting in Canada. I am appealing for fair consideration of his application to remain here as a landed immigrant, but the house will be interested to know that the department of immigration, through a man I could identify, an employee of the department in Toronto, notified this Greek citizen on Friday last by telephone to be ready to leave Canada next Friday, June 16. I should not like to accuse the department of immigration of having already made up their mind before they hear the matter that I wish to discuss, but it does appear somewhat as though an appeal court had said to an appellant: "We will hear your appeal tomorrow but be ready to go to Kingston penitentiary the day after".
The last time I had occasion to take up a matter with the parliamentary secretary to the minister I can assure you I received the kindest consideration, and I am expecting the same tonight.
On June 6 I asked this question in the House of Commons, as reported at page 1191 of Hansard:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question which I would like to address to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration. Can he give us any estimate as to how many United States citizens may be visiting Canada at the present time in order to avoid the army draft?
I asked that question because of this Greek who is 23 years of age, unmarried and living
June 12, 1967

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion with an uncle in the riding of York-Humber. This Greek came to Canada as a visitor last August. When he came here he came to visit relatives, fully intending to return to Greece. At Christmastime he got in touch with me to ask if I could get an extension of his three month visit so that he could spend Christmas and New Year with his relatives here. This the Department of Manpower and Immigration readily granted.
I never heard from the Greek man until about three weeks ago when I ascertained for the first time that he had made an appeal for landed immigrant status and had been turned down by the immigration department and by the immigration appeal board. Interestingly enough, he was turned down in the first instance on March 8 and appealed some time later in the month, was turned down and ordered deported.
I must bring to the attention of the house and of the Department of Manpower and Immigration that on April 10 and 11 the Minister of Manpower and Immigration issued two statements which I have in my hand, about changes which have been made in the qualifications with respect to landed immigrant status. Those changes are such that the Greek can qualify to remain in Canada as a landed immigrant.
Much more important is the fact that on April 21 there was a revolution in Greece and the country is now in the hands of the army.
When I raised this point with the Minister of Manpower and Immigration in the latter part of May and told him of this young lad who has done service in the Greek army and who does not wish to return to Greece because his country is in the hands of the army, and because the premier has been deposed, and because they do not have democratic government in Greece, I was assured with the answer: "We can assure you that everything is fine in Greece."
On May 29 I received a letter signed by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration-so it must be official-in which this appears:
In addition to the circumstances of the individual case, you will be interested to know that the department has made enquiries through the Department of External Affairs regarding current conditions in Greece. Our ambassador in Athens reports that conditions are quite stable, and that persons returning to Greece have no reason to fear hardship or difficulty.
That is terrific. With the army in control I imagine conditions are stable in Greece. I can tell the Minister of Manpower and Immigration that conditions are very stable in

Washington and New York, in Buffalo and Los Angeles. The government is in control in the United States. Why do we not force the 300 odd Americans who are over here dodging the draft in the Viet Nam war to go back to the United States? Why force this one Greek who has already done his two years in the army, who has already served his country, to go back to a land that is in the hands of the army?
If conditions in Greece are so stable why are we keeping a Canadian army contingent in Cyprus. I know that Cyprus is an independent republic, but also remember that the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) and the hon. member who once represented Lac-Saint-Jean (Mr. Lessard) who is no longer with us, kept asking what is to happen to Canadian troops when the Greeks land in Cyprus? The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) said that the plans for the evacuation of Canadian troops when trouble starts in Cyprus are complete.
Why send the Greek back to Greece if there is some likelihood of the Greek army invading Cyprus, where we now have Canadian troops. I submit that if we are not ordering the 300 United States citizens back to their country we have no right to order the one Greek back to Greece.
A member of the Canadian federal cabinet went on a United States network and admitted that there are perhaps 300 draft dodgers in this country. I have nothing against them; they have to live with themselves. I remember that between 1914 and 1917 Canadians went to the United States, so perhaps we should not mind if a few people from the United States now come to Canada. Americans can quite easily come to Canada and lose themselves in the population of this country, but a Greek has to provide a visitor's visa when he comes in; his every address is known, as is his every movement. I say, let us be fair to the Greeks in the same way as we are trying to be fair with the Americans. Let us not make fish of one and fowl of the other.

speakeroldname: Mr. John C. Munro (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immi-gation):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
maintopic: IMMIGRATION-U.S. CITIZENS IN CANADA TO ESCAPE ARMY DRAFT
speechtext:
The hon. member for York-Humber (Mr. Cowan) has referred to present conditions in Greece. The department has made inquiries through the Department of External Affairs and we are informed that the ordinary
June 12, 1967

Greek citizen who is returning to his country, voluntarily or otherwise, has no reason to fear persecution.
The hon. member also has referred to my department's policy toward aliens who may be subject to military call-up in their homelands. An individual's status with regard to compulsory military service in his own country has no bearing upon his admissibility to Canada either as an immigrant or as a visitor; nor is he subject to removal from Canada because of unfulfilled military obligations in his country of citizenship. In any event, in the particular case of Mr. Sistanis, the young man already has completed his period of compulsory military service in Greece and we have no evidence that he is subject to any further compulsory service there.
Mr. Sistanis entered Canada as a visitor and later applied for immigrant status here. He did not comply with the conditions for such a change of status and was asked to leave Canada. His failure to do so resulted in the holding of an inquiry and the issuance of an order for his deportation. The immigration appeal board dismissed his appeal against the order and recommended that the deportation be carried out. The minister can find no reason to change their decision.
Whether or not Mr. Sistanis might qualify for admission to Canada from Greece when new immigrant selection criteria come into force is beside the point. He does not qualify under the conditions the minister announced to the house last July. As hon. members know, the minister is proposing to change and, I believe, improve the criteria for the selection of immigrants. The minister made it
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion clear to the parliamentary committee, however, that it will be some months before our officers are in a position to apply new rules and procedures. No one can say at this point how Mr. Sistanis, if he were in Greece, would stand under those rules. Therefore, it would be unfair to other people if, on the basis of the personal view of the member for York-Humber, the minister were to act now on the assumption that this particular young man is going to be admissible.
It must be clear to any practical person that we would have chaos if the minister were to exercise his discretion to defer settling a case until it could be dealt with under the new criteria, as anything more than a rare exception for particularly strong reasons. The minister is prepared to do this when special hardship may otherwise be involved. Indeed the minister has done so already in a few cases, but he is satisfied that Mr. Sistanis does not come within that category. Therefore the immigration officials will arrange for his deportation as soon as possible.
If he wishes to apply in Athens, in the normal manner, for readmission to Canada as an immigrant when the new selection criteria come into force, the minister wishes to assure the hon. member that his deportation will not be held against him in any way.
